By integrating this framework with a flexible mesh topology, even more accurate results can be achieved in multi-phase flows and FSI simulations, as shown in several benchmark tests. Furthermore, a multi-phase FSI simulation was even able to accurately match the results of an experimental study on a moving fish, showcasing the potential of this SPH framework to provide biologically authentic simulations of aquatic organisms.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent of the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks, achieving an impressive speedup due to a lower asymptotic complexity of $O(N^{3/2}K^{1/2}\log{P})$ with $N$, $K$, and $P$ representing the number of data points, clusters, and data dimensions, respectively.

A recently created TTS model called FastPitch can change pitch, but the quality of the speech made with it gets significantly worse when it's given pitch values far from its average pitch.  We suggest using a new method of pitch augmentation based on speech characteristics that doesn't cause a decline in quality, which makes it easier to control FastPitch's pitch.  We also propose a way to improve FastPitch so it can handle a wider range of pitches without any negative effects, which makes it easier to use.  We tested our method with speech samples from various languages, including English, German, Czech, Spanish, Mandarin Chinese, and Icelandic, and compared it to the original FastPitch model.  We found that our method significantly improves FastPitch's ability to be controlled, which is great for using it in applications where pitch needs to be changed.  We also found that the majority of listeners preferred our method over the original FastPitch when it came to sound quality.

This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal object-based reasoning challenges in videos by employing object persistence principles. Our proposed solution includes an 'hopper', a multi-hop reasoning model incorporating transformer architecture, which determines an object's location and activity history in each frame. By iteratively applying this information, it accurately identifies objects' spatial and temporal connections across video sequences. To evaluate the hopper's performance and testing object-based reasoning across different scenarios, we introduce several challenges ranging from easy to difficult. When tested against strong baseline models and refined combinations of these challenges, the hopper demonstrates superior reasoning capabilities, exceeding the combined performance by significant margins, up to a staggering 14.8% improvement in cases considered most demanding. By dissecting the hopper's multi-hop decision-making process and analyzing its errors, this research lays the groundwork for future research to address spatiotemporal reasoning. We will make all developed resources available to the research community through https://github.com/asharakeh/smart-cities/tree/smart-cities.

Our research investigates lepton-pair production coupled with bottom quarks at the Large Hadron Collider using theoretical predictions from next-to-leading order QCD. The studies encompass various factors, including the influence of finite collider energy, additional particles, and the inherent structure of the proton. The investigations draw upon Monte Carlo simulations, parton distribution functions, and cross-section and differential quantity calculations. The research compares different methods for determining the W boson mass, specifically those involving matrix element reweighting, the likelihood density method, and the neural network technique using various observables. The findings reveal that recent experimental data collected by the ATLAS collaboration can be utilized to derive a precise value for the W boson mass, specifically, $80.356\pm 0.0617$ GeV.

Remote-controlled vehicles called Telepresence robots have gained popularity in recent years due to their affordable pricing and ability to offer remote interactions in various settings, making them easy to deploy and navigate through everyday environments. A crucial factor for achieving high remote presence quality is understanding the end-user experience when using these robots via a network connection, especially when considering factors such as network delays, jitters, and other issues that can impact the experience quality. To address this need, this study introduces a new evaluation method for assessing the quality of experience (QoE) of remote navigation through these robots by utilizing a survey-based approach that provides more accurate results compared to existing methods. For maximum interaction accuracy, a 30-minute video demonstration is provided to participants, which includes actual robot traffic and a virtual network disturbance scenario to test their responses. By assuming a linear combination of two quality metrics, a predictive model can estimate the user's visual experience quality, which correlates with established performance measures, specifically the Mean Opinion Score (MOS). For evaluating the user's experience with Telepresence robots, a quantitative study was conducted with 82 participants provided with various scenarios, which showed the proposed model's accuracy in predicting QoE and accurately quantifying the user's experience, which showed consistent results across 60 participants. Which highlights the importance of user experience research in achieving high remote presence quality.

In this study, we revisit the core features of two Bayesian hierarchical regression models, thoroughly analyzing their full conditional distributions during Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling. We clarify and resolve ambiguities in earlier implementations of these models, addressing issues in prior distributions, conjugate priors, and conditional distributions in both the linear regression model and its hierarchical extension. We demonstrate how this work can serve as a foundational resource for Bayesian hierarchical regression and encourage the development of additional models by expanding on our mathematical framework.

The game "Mafia," also known as "Werewolf," is a party-based competition between two opposing groups. Citizens and mafia members are the main groups. Each phase in the game, consisting of day and night segments, allows for various actions to be taken, with lynching occurring during the day phase. Mafia members possess special abilities that distinguish them from the citizens, who are the dominant group due to their higher numbers. Researchers have developed a mathematical model that represents the game's progression as a discrete-time pure death process. They have found precise equations describing the mafia's chances of winning and the overall game's progression, also exploring their discrete properties and continuous-time approximations. Studies have shown that only a small number of mafia members, equivalent to the square root of the total player count, can grant the mafia and the citizens an equal probability of winning. Additionally, the outcome of the game heavily relies on whether the total number of players is even or odd.

Several planetary systems have multiple giant planets, and research aims to
understand how their properties develop and the effects of accretion. We examine
the co-growth of two Jovian planets and its influence on their mass and the
 surrounding protoplanetary disk. We created models of planetary development,
 accounting for the exchange of material between the planets and the disk, and
 varied the ratio of accreted gas to planet mass. Studies revealed a correlation
 between the ratio of accreted gas and the planets' final mass, and this ratio
 affects their orbital periods. If one planet efficiently accretes gas, the other
 will likely have lower mass and a wider orbital separation. Furthermore, our
 models show changes in the disk's mass due to accretion by the planets. In
 scenarios with efficient gas accretion, the planets will have massive cores and
 the disk will lose mass, whereas in cases with less efficient gas accretion,
 the planets will have smaller cores and the disk will gain mass. These findings
 suggest that multiple planets developing simultaneously may alter the disk's mass
 and lead to variations in planets' mass and orbital periods.

The electrical conductivity of an ensemble of nanomaterials on a macroscopic scale
depends on complex interactions between the constituent nanoscale entities and an
environment that can facilitate or impede charge or heat transport.  Understanding
these interactions is crucial for both designing nanomaterials with enhanced
transportabilities and analyzing experimental results.  In particular, various
theoretical models have been proposed for explaining inter-nanotube electronic transport
mechanisms, but few studies have experimentally validated the underlying models.
Utilizing both macroscopic and microscopic measurements, our study examines the
single-crystal armchair carbon nanotube film conductivity and provides clear evidence
of phonon-assisted transport through comparison of conductivity measurements with
models based on the linear response theory of inter-nanoparticle coupling.  By analyzing
the film's conductivity in vacuum and ambient environments, our results show that only
the model incorporating phonon-assisted transport aligns with experimental observations,
whereas the models assuming purely elastic or repulsive couplings fail to match the
experimental findings.  Moreover, our study demonstrates that measurements of both
macroscopic films and individual nanomaterials are interdependent and require a dual
approach for confirmation.

This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple subspaces. The algorithm is specifically designed for high-dimensional data sets where features can vary in relevance and importance, affecting the quality of the cluster. To overcome this limitation, a variable feature weight operation is incorporated into the fuzzy k-means method. The proposed VFWFM algorithm enables the identification of optimal clusters while allowing for the characterization of each subset by a minimum entropy value. The entropy measure is used to evaluate the randomness and diversity of data within each cluster. The effectiveness of the VFWFM method is demonstrated through multiple numerical simulations and real-world applications.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial components of various neural networks and ensemble learning systems. However, traditional algorithms used to train MoE models are often stuck in local optima, preventing them from reaching optimal solutions. In an effort to break this deadlock, we introduce a groundbreaking method, dynamic gateway sampling (DGS), alongside a straightforward optimization technique that works in tandem with existing gradient descent algorithms. This novel approach ensures that the dual problem of the optimal solution is always found. Moreover, our new algorithm outperforms its predecessors in various experiments and achieves a notable gain of up to 45% in test accuracy when used with residual gates.

This set of notes offers a standalone review of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the theory of Jacobians and Prym varieties, which were presented at the 2020 Representation Theory and Modular Forms Workshop at Towson University.

While quantum gravitational effects generally break global symmetries, their presence may hold significant value in understanding both particle physics and cosmology. Discovering well-maintained global symmetries in nature could provide a valuable insight into quantum gravity. A global $U(1)$ symmetry in nature is a plausible candidate, and one way to explore this symmetry is through measurements of cosmic birefringence, which modifies photon polarization and a large-scale structure formation momentum distribution. Research has established a constraint on birefringence, and we have established a limit on symmetry breaking, which matches the bounds set by photon birefringence measurements in certain scenarios but is stronger in others. Additionally, our study highlights the potential for future cosmological birefringence measurements to explore the nature of quantum gravity.

Our research presents new findings based on far ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the globular cluster NGC 4147 obtained with three specific filters onboard the AstroSat satellite. These findings were further confirmed by cross-checking the source's identification and photometric analysis from existing optical data, as well as ultraviolet and visible photometry from the AstroSat archive. A total of 57 sources were detected within the 1 arcminute radius of the cluster, of which 46 can be matched with sources in the General Catalogue and/or the Tycho-2 Survey, and 21 others are new candidate members of NGC 4147. Further analysis of these candidate members, the brightest two FUV sources, and the brightest two visible sources may offer insights into the evolution of hot stars. In a separate observation and subsequent analysis of a single Giant Blue Star, no X-ray emission was detected above the detection limit of our instruments within the 3 sigma confidence level. These findings conform to the current understanding of the expected characteristics of the magnetic field in a cluster of this type. Furthermore, the frequency and distribution of magnetic activity among the rotating hot stars within the cluster also conform to existing research in this domain.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) with the ability to draw from past experiences like humans. Past research aimed to develop DNNs capable of adapting to multiple tasks simultaneously, with some studies suggesting generalization through transferability. There have been numerous claims and assumptions regarding the transferability of DNNs, but many remain unsubstantiated or conflicting. Some argue that past experiences do not affect DNNs, claiming that pre-trained models merely serve as a starting point for new training. Others suggest that DNNs can learn abstract patterns, which may not directly apply to the target domain but aid in learning. Furthermore, some find that past experiences can hinder DNNs by distracting from the actual task at hand. Despite these claims, an in-depth examination of the transferability of DNNs is lacking. In this article, we revisit two presumed consensuses of the transferability in deep learning: (1) the idea that DNNs can achieve better performance through intermediate supervision during pre-training, (2) the assumption that the performance of DNNs would decrease or remain the same if past experiences were removed from the pre-training phase. Our study aims to validate these claims through the systematic evaluation of the transferability of DNNs using representative datasets across multiple fields, thereby contributing to the advancement of DTL. Our findings indicate that the initial consensus is incorrect and the latter is valid once biases are removed from the pre-trained

In various scenarios, such as mobilization, pandemic mitigation, and advertising, the swift dissemination of information and social behaviors are paramount. Despite thorough examinations of massive cascade dynamics across social media and online networks, few studies have delve into the initial phases of these events. By modeling information spread on a network using nonlinear equations, our research reveals that the average rate of this process is substantially higher in networks with a loose community structure than in those with a more compact one. Furthermore, our results illustrate the complex interplay between network dynamics and the inherent organization of its components, highlighting the pivotal role of modularity in enhancing cascade velocity.

Under specific conditions from Floer theory, we derive numerical measures indicating the proximity of two Lagrangians based on their angular separation, and these measurements depend on how close those Lagrangian angles are to being perfectly aligned. Some outcomes resulting from these conditions are a definitive uniqueness proof for special Lagrangians and a detailed criterion describing the process by which a collection of varifolds converges towards a special Lagrangian, with this criterion itself dependent on Lagrangian angles.

The reliability of a discrete-time channel model that uses a standard method of perturbation
is numerically investigated for cases without signal amplification. We assess the distance between 
discrete nonlinear interference points and find that this distance can be employed to estimate 
the effective memory length of the communication channel.

The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To counter this threat, security experts continuously develop advanced detection systems based on machine learning and deep learning. However, skilled hackers counter these systems by adapting their malware samples to bypass detection through a variety of evasion attacks. A unique aspect of Android devices lies in the installation of third-party apps from sources other than the Google Play Store, known as app stores. This study focuses on problem-space evasion attacks on Android devices, assessing how malware existences within a space of possible malicious configurations. The study aims to provide an overview of these attacks, highlighting their key characteristics, examples, and comparing different evasion approaches beyond the same domain. Furthermore, the study outlines potential future research paths focused on problem-space evasion attacks on Android devices.

Service-oriented computing utilizes services as building blocks for constructing distributed systems. Traditionally, orchestrating cloud-based services centered around problem-solving, but the advent of microservices has led to a shift towards using services as means of problem-solving. This shift inevitably results in a higher complexity in orchestrating such services, especially when diverse service types are involved. This paper proposes a novel approach to a consistent workflow-based model for high-level orchestration purposes. A practical tool, Ozy, is demonstrated to exemplify this model, enabling a simplified and unified approach to orchestrating a multitude of services through example use cases.

Recent experimental observations supporting the particle-hole symmetric Pfaffian topological order are challenged by a reoccurring phase of unusual quantized nature, which is gapped in the thermodynamic limit.  Unlike other known phases such as pfaffian, antipfaffian, and color-code phases, this new phase exhibits no particle-hole symmetry, and instead, its ground state features a unique form of energy splitting that increases with the magnetic field's strength.  A gapped phase emerging from the Pf-Gf phase transition in the intermediate Landau level-mixing regime is proposed to be the root of the observed reentrant phase transition, which is characterized by distinct energy splittings in both the weak and strong magnetic field regimes.  Moreover, this new phase is predicted to be experimentally identifiable through its unique signatures in the energy spectrum of trial wave functions constructed via the Giamarchi-Schrieffer mechanism, which matches the findings of recent experiments on the 5/2 Landau level, and differs from those of both pfaffian and antipfaffian phases.

Our investigation into whether primordial black holes could be the dark matter, excluding those produced during inflation, led to a hypothesis involving a specific type of black hole called the Thakurta black hole. However, a thorough examination of the physical properties of this type of black hole suggests that its characteristics are incompatible with those observed in the electrical binary merger GRB 200415A. Furthermore, even if such black holes were created through an unforeseen mechanism, their properties would be distinct from those of the 22 kg primordial black holes detected by the LIGO-Virgo Collaboration, and therefore would not affect the current constraints regarding the abundance of primordial black holes, which remain unchanged at $1.35\times10^{-8}$.

The complexity of gaps and spiral patterns in a young stellar environment reveals a detailed history of accretion and evolution of a forming planetary system. To better understand the formation of planets through pebble accretion theory, our study aims to investigate the impact of undulating density on the planet formation process. By simulating a planetary model within a periodically varying, linear gravitational potential, created by a stellar perturbation, our results show that the fluctuating density of a planetary material affects the planet's mass accumulation. The simulations propose that these variations in density could explain the multiple-planet patterns observed in the distribution of exoplanets. The simulations also provide new insights into the conditions for pebble isolation and the transfer of mass from pebbles to planets, and how these processes change with the planet's distance from its host star. The simulated outcomes suggest that planets forming in regions with intense radiation from their host stars tend to have lower masses compared to those formed in areas with moderate radiation. The simulated model further suggests a correlation between the mass of a forming planet and its orbital distance, which could explain a particular pattern in the distribution of exoplanets known as the mass-radius valley. The simulated outcomes also propose a possible range of timescales for pebble isolation, which could explain a particular part of a forming planetary material that could eventually become part of small, rocky planets.

Extremely large, overparameterized models have achieved impressive success. In this research, we examine whether the requirement for massive models might be partly attributed to computational limitations inherent to the learner itself. We concentrate on learning linear regression models, investigating how the learner's computational resources influence the number of parameters needed. We show that there is a minimum number of columns in the design matrix that must be sampled or estimated, depending on the computational capacity of the learner, to guarantee accurate model finding. We considered two primary computational constraints - the limitation on the maximum runtime and the restriction on the maximum approximation error for any given data pair. We explored various scenarios, including when the bias and noise in the data series are known or unknown. We also extended our findings to approximately learning, a concept initially explored by Andreyev and Tsuruvalya. Our results suggest that the minimum number of columns in the design matrix is logarithmically proportional to the learner's computational constraints. We also argue that the established upper bounds on the number of columns can be considered as moderate computational constraints. Furthermore, we illustrate that the upper bounds we obtained for the sampled design matrix apply to any matrix, including those with a specific number of rows and columns. We also prove that the established upper bounds for the sampled design matrix apply to any matrix with a number of rows greater than or equal to $2$. We also argue that the established upper bounds for the sampled design matrix apply to any matrix with a number of rows greater than or equal

Three results concerning the presence of Bohr sets in two-element sumsets have been established. More specifically, considering a countable discrete abelian group $G$ and let $\Lambda$ be a subgroup of $G$ of finite rank. In an earlier paper by the second author with G. Malijer, it was demonstrated that any set of measure $\delta$ within $G$ is contained within a Bohr set with measure $\epsilon$. This new paper expands on that by providing a revised version of that result as well as two distinct generalisations involving the number of summands and the properties of the subgroup $\Lambda$.

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have multiple transportation options at their disposal. To remain competitive, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates against minimizing detours for users. We propose a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to tackle this challenge, leveraging insights from established route paths to identify and exclude non-viable solutions, thus enhancing lower-bound estimates for arrival times. Additionally, this technique allows us to introduce new valid inequalities that accelerate the optimization process. We conducted an extensive computational analysis involving up to 120 customers and found that our method consistently outperforms a traditional mixed-integer programming formulation by finding better solutions and reducing processing times dramatically.

This study explores multi-modal pretraining techniques for product data in E-commerce, addressing limitations in current methods which struggle to capture detailed product attributes like price and texture. We introduce K3M, a novel method incorporating knowledge modal for multi-modal pretraining. K3M utilizes three modalities - image, text and knowledge, each generating three pretraining objectives to complement the model. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance on various E-commerce datasets when compared to existing methods in benchmarking studies.

A significant function in most algorithms for analyzing brain scans is attributed to unsupervised learning, particularly in non-linear exploration. A novel approach, Deep InfoMax (DIM), offers considerable potential for examining brain structure adaptability. In this paper, the potential of modified DIM models is compared to conventional supervised networks, such as AlexNet and ResNet, in predicting progression to Alzheimer's disease using classification tasks and brain scans from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. While DIM models show promising results for uncovering underlying patterns and their ability to detect early indicators of Alzheimer's disease, they fall short of toppling the supremacy of well-established, parameter-heavy architectures like ResNet in prediction accuracy. Nevertheless, our research indicates that DIM models can be effectively applied to investigating the causes and mechanisms of neurological diseases.

Natural Language Processing employs a crucial task called text classification, which sequential models efficiently handle, though their linear design hinders the processing of texts containing intricate interactions among components. To overcome this limitation, this research introduces an innovative, interactive-based recurrent framework named LINRNN, capable of incorporating multiple attention mechanisms. By integrating interactions into the recurrent neural network, LINRNN's non-linear structure enables it to detect complex patterns within texts more effectively. LINRNN's performance was evaluated across three diverse text classification datasets, with the results indicating significant improvements over baseline models and other leading deep learning methods.

We examine the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and interactions within a two-orbital Hubbard model on a square lattice, employing the variational Monte Carlo method. An effective spin-orbit constant $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ is considered in the wave function, focusing primarily on quarter-filled electrons. We find that $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ correlates directly with the bare $\lambda$ and depends on electron interactions represented by the parameter $(U'-J')$, within a broad range in the paramagnetic phase, where $U'$ represents the inter-orbital interaction and $J'$ represents the pair hopping interaction. Increasing interactions within this phase causes a shift to a state resembling an effective single band system, in which the upper band becomes uninhabited due to amplified $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$. Additionally, magnetic order considerations and carrier doping effects on $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ are analyzed, revealing that it increases in a highly correlated area surrounding the Mott transition and thus requires accounting for interactions beyond Hartree-Fock theory to describe the SOC accurately.

A metastable dark matter candidate emerges as a natural consequence of a
conformal transformation between the Einstein metric, where gravitons are normalised states,
and the Jordan metric governing the coupling between matter and gravity in the early universe.
As a result, the graviton field acquires a mass, manifesting as a degree of dark matter with a
mass-dependent interaction strength that increases in proportion to the graviton mass.
Within the context of the running coupling limit, the condition $m_{dark} < m_{graviton}$ must be met.
Assuming that the graviton mass spans a range from $10^{-3}$ eV to $10^{-14}$ eV, a broad
sub-MeV dark matter mass spectrum is predicted, spanning from a few hundred keV to a few MeV.
A related metastable dark light candidate also exists, arising as a natural consequence of the
dark matter sector, and characterised by a mass proportional to the square of the graviton
mass. In this light, the favored parameter space of the vector-assisted dark matter model
experiences relaxation, albeit the relic abundance of the dark matter remains largely unaltered.
Importantly, observation-free regions of parameter space emerge, and a distinctive
anisotropic distortion pattern in the CMB results from the presence of dark matter, differing
from the standard QCD-motivated relic abundance prediction. A comprehensive analysis has been
carried out on detection prospects via direct

To ensure that AI-powered medical devices operate safely and efficiently in diverse environments before being released to the public, accurately assessing their performance in varying scenarios is crucial. Given the regulatory restrictions on medical software and the scarcity of comprehensive labeled medical datasets, our approach revolves around predicting a model's performance in an unfamiliar setting using its predicted responses alone, without requiring any modifications to its training process or assumptions about its original data source. This "black-box" model assessment technique is evaluated in the context of a distribution shift, with a particular focus on its practical application to medical datasets. Conformal prediction empowers our prediction model to estimate the distribution shift, while also providing a concrete prediction accuracy assurance. This method's effectiveness is substantiated through experiments conducted on various medical image classification datasets, with particular emphasis on the transition from otoscope images to real-world clinical images, demonstrating its versatility in diverse scenarios.

High-fidelity simulations involving atomic-level details are now being extensively employed to study nucleic acid structures due to their high precision and resolution in space and time, lasting weeks. However, such simulations have a significant drawback - they are extremely slow and expensive, limiting the scope of viable targets in free and bound states for further analysis. Advanced simulation techniques, such as enhanced sampling methods (e.g., metadynamics) high-throughput systems (e.g, parallel processing), and various algorithms (e.g, umbrella sampling) have been used to overcome these limitations by exploring a wider range of states and structures in nucleic acids. Despite these efforts, the design of suitable high-dimensional sampling strategies remains a challenge. Our team has developed a rigorous sampling approach for DNA (ResDNA) which focuses on the orientation of DNA bases with respect to their surroundings. Our results indicate that ResDNA leads to significant enhancements in the conformational sampling of DNA over traditional methods in several instances, enabling the accurate prediction of key characteristics related to DNA transport, self-recognition, and interactions with other molecules (e.g, anti-cancer drugs). Our study shows that the ResDNA technique offers potential applications in the analysis of nucleic acid structures in its bound and free states, with a range of possibilities extending far beyond what is shown here.

The Asymmetric Numeral System (ANS) was a significant contribution to entropy encoding, offering improved performance through a greater rate range and simpler implementation. However, the article provides a precise analysis of its rate distortion function, determines its efficiency, and demonstrates that its advantages come at a lower complexity cost compared to the best entropy encodings.

The dielectric characteristics of micro- and mesoporous materials are heavily influenced by the composition and electrical responses of their pore liquids. In the case of cement-based materials and similar systems, the pore liquid is often subject to varying conditions that affect its dielectric behavior. This work provides experimental and theoretical estimates of the dielectric properties of aqueous solutions containing substances that cement-pore-solutions typically comprise. This research aims to enhance the precision of predictive models involving cement-based materials by incorporating accurate dielectric data. Furthermore, the findings may broaden the understanding of dielectric responses in complex systems where the composition of the pore liquid plays a significant role.

In our earlier work, the range of heavy-antiheavy hadronic molecules was determined, and a predictive model based on resonance saturation was established. This model has been successful in explaining several observed hadronic molecules such as $X(3872)$, $Y(4260)$, and the $P_c$ states, and its predictions for heavy-heavy hadronic molecules seem even more likely. The fact that heavy-antiheavy hadronic molecules with experimental evidence can be described by the same dominant interaction, implies that heavy-heavy ones also exist. The additional predictions from our model include new heavy-heavy states at various masses, and the observation that heavy-antiheavy states can be reinterpreted as heavy-heavy ones by changing their decay particle spectra, and in some cases their mass.

Research on military drones is growing in importance as a swarm can be a
useful asset in military operations, and recent studies have expanded the
field from theoretical foundations to practical applications in conflicts.
However, accessible analysis of the progress in this area is scarce, and
the usual academic databases with comprehensive citation indices can fall
short. This study investigates the development drivers of military swarms
by analyzing the trajectory of influential research in the field through
a textual search across the IEEE platform, employing the BibTeX database.
By employing the Bibliographic Coupling method with Natural Language
Processing, our research reveals key publications and cites them, and
identifies leading researchers, as well as the journals and conferences
driving progress, along with the corresponding keywords.

When performing cosmological inferences based on the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions, standard analyses usually only consider a specific feature related to baryon acoustic oscillations. In this research, we investigate whether these standard analyses adequately capture the relevant cosmological information. To address this, we directly fitted the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions, including cross-correlations with quasars, without simplifying them, and then evaluated BAO information within this full set of data. Our results show that omitting cross-correlations with quasars or only considering a specific feature of the autocorrelation function, like the one with a feature at small scales, significantly reduces the precision of parameter estimation and increases the potential for bias, especially when trying to constrain non-Newtonian velocity bias. To fully utilize the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions, it is essential to both consider cross-correlations with quasars and expand the analysed scale range to around or below a pixel of 4 Mpc/h and include smaller scales, below a pixel of 2 Mpc/h), while also carefully handling potential non-Newtonian velocity bias. Our code that implements these changes is freely accessible and provides an easy-to-use tool for making these modifications.

Researchers at Fermilab have successfully conducted an experiment where a beam of particles undergoes an unconventional manipulation, swapping its horizontal and longitudinal beam patterns at the A0 Photoinjector. The new experimental setup, featuring a specially designed deflector accompanied by curved beamsplitting components, has enabled the first observation of a distinct phase shift between the particle beam's trajectory and its time-of-flight.

A fundamental component of various technologies, including surveillance, robotic navigation, and self-driving systems, is pedestrian trajectory prediction, and significant advancements have been made in this field. Nevertheless, past studies still have two main drawbacks. Firstly, they have tended to overlook the inherent characteristics of sequences and treated each prediction as an isolated event, rather than recognizing they pertain to linked sequences. Secondly, they have not adequately incorporated the evolving natures of predicted trajectories, nor the socially interconnected aspects of multiple pedestrians within a prediction context. In order to tackle these challenges, this study presents Sliding Sequential Categorical VAE (Sliding CVAE), a novel technique that leverages a hierarchical approach, with two interconnected objectives. Firstly, it optimizes the variation of sequential predictions within a sliding window framework, with a categorical approach that incorporates a dynamic R-retwork layer. Secondly, it develops a novel topological autoencoder, with time variant socially-aware thinking for rethinking predicted trajectories, in a way that dynamically allows for forward and backward thinking. In addition to this, we have developed a new dataset, Edinburgh Interaction Part-2, with a focus on interacting groups of people, and utilized it for trajectory prediction, along with multiple other datasets for evaluation purposes. Results have shown significant accuracy improvements with proposed approaches, with accuracy rates being as high as 17% higher than the best models employed previously, especially for the accuracy of mean intersection over union.

We apply information-theoretic measures of complexity to study the behavior of basic neural networks, specifically Boltzmann machines with one hidden layer. Our investigations into these measures, such as entropy, mutual information, and complexity, based on their definitions by Lizier, reveal how they relate to each other and how they maximize or minimize them affects the training process of the network. Contrary to initial expectations, increasing mutual information and complexity led to decreased performance, while maintaining entropy resulted in decent performance, but not optimal. These findings are published in a paper that provides a thorough explanation of the methods used, followed by a discussion of the results and suggestions for future research.

This paper showcases initial research on an innovative technique for facilitating communication between humans and a swarm of robots. Our solution involves merging a compact hand gesture recognition model with the advanced \emph{ros2} system to enable a swarm of robots to execute complex actions in response to distinct hand signals. Our experiment, utilizing a dataset of 20 distinct gross motor hand gestures and 8 arm postures, achieved a remarkable 89.4\% accuracy mark. This promising development has the potential to create a seamless, two-way dialogue between humans and swarms of robots, even in real-world applications.

The study aims to assess the performance of composite deep learning models consisting of Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks for identifying diverse White Blood Cell types, a feat that could revolutionize automated medical diagnosis and blood analysis in pharmaceutical and healthcare settings by analyzing image samples, thereby aiding in disease diagnosis for patients.

A key strategy for efficiently preparing the ground state of a quantum system is counterdiabatic driving (CD). This method directly drives the system's ground state by carefully controlling its evolution, effectively bypassing any competing excited states that might be encountered during the process. Although CD is an ideal driving protocol, determining the required driving terms can be complex and involve significant numerical challenges. In this work, an innovative variation of CD is presented, where the driving terms can be approximated through minimization of a cost function, leveraging variational quantum classical algorithms (VQCs). The development of this approach is illustrated by applying it to the Hubbard model, where the formation of a singlet ground state is achieved through a SWAP-based quantum classical algorithm. The required driving terms can be found with reasonable computational efficiency using moderately sized quantum circuits, whose size scales logarithmically with the desired accuracy.

Color-neutral images are a cornerstone in various image processing applications such as image compression, feature extraction, and printing due to their role in tone mapping. However, valuable image data gets lost when transitioning color images to their grayscale or de-colorized counterparts, as this process eliminates the visual cues harnessed by color information. This research presents an innovative, efficient image de-colorization technique that uses the concept of color temperature to preserve the overall visual integrity of images while retaining their color-based properties. A fast and robust optimization method is employed to extract multiple segmental color temperature patterns that, in turn, independently map colors to the grayscale scale using an optimized color temperature-LUT. Experimental findings confirm that this proposed technique successfully recovers the full image content, including its color information, as its accuracy surpasses the performance of base-line EEDC method by 2-3 dB under various metrics, including MS-SSIM, MS-NCSE, and CAM.

This research develops an expression to decompose infinitely differentiable complex-valued functions into a sum of exponentials along with a corresponding error term. Building upon this, a corresponding infinite series is derived for functions in $C^\infty$, which converges to the original function under specified conditions on the remainder term. Subsequent applications of these results enable the computation of certain infinite series connected to Stirling numbers.

Given a surface S equipped with a metric d, where R and 1/r are both finite and satisfy d's curvature being pinched between 0 and 1, it is demonstrated that an almost conformal harmonic map from a surface to (S, d) can be extended to a conformal isometry if it meets certain conditions previously established by Boots-Brinker. This result is then applied in the case where (S, d) is diffeomorphic to a sphere, which leads to an extension of the well-known uniformization theorem, providing a new proof of Bers' theorem. Additionally, it is shown that harmonic maps can be used to reprove Branner and Bruck's result on the iterates of the branched coverings associated to the dynamics of the complex dilations around points with attracting behavior.

We've created a state-of-the-art laser-plasma platform to study fundamental photon-photon collision phenomena, such as the linear Breit-Wheeler process using real photons, by leveraging the Gemini laser facility at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory. Our recent experiments at the facility have involved taking data for single and double pair production in collisions between real photons and electrons. The measurements, based on nearly 10^8 pair events, have demonstrated high precision and good agreement with theoretical predictions. Moreover, this platform has provided clean, high-intensity photon beams, facilitating accurate measurements of photon-photon collisions. The success of these experiments has paved the way for future studies of complex Compton scattering at the facility.

In a forthcoming letter, we examine how sensitive the Two Higgs Doublet Model is to a crucial parameter, $m_{12}$, which breaks the symmetry softly and impacts the Higgs boson decays significantly. Along with other vital model parameters like the Higgs boson masses and the Higgs vacuum expectation values ratio, $m_{12}$ determines how effectively Higgs bosons decay and interact with Standard Model particles. By focusing on the lightest Higgs boson decaying into two photons, which are observed with characteristics resembling those of Standard Model particles under a specific alignment condition, this study aims to establish the bounds that current measurements can place on $m_{12}$ in different regions of the Two Higgs Doublet Model's parameter space. Our exploration of various model scenarios, such as four distinct Yukawa types and the possibility of accommodating a revised world average for the W boson mass in the Higgs boson mass spectrum, offers deeper insights into these constraints. Furthermore, this study develops upon previous studies by incorporating all available constraints from Higgs boson decays without prioritizing their implementation.

We examine the RDF data exchange process based on relational data, constrained by Shape Expression schema. Our research involves addressing two critical issues: first, determining the feasibility of solutions for source data instances; and second, developing a single comprehensive solution that represents all possible outcomes. To achieve this, we incorporate typed IRI constructors to form RDF IRIs from relational values and translate Shape Expression constraints into target dependencies using special relations that encapsulate shape coverage and data constraint conditions. Additionally, we have identified certain data exchange scenarios with unconditional coverage, where every source data instance can produce a valid result. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that for each data exchange with conditional coverage, there exists an intermediate relation with a restricted dataset that can generate the same results as the original data exchange. However, determining whether such an intermediate relation necessarily exists for every data exchange with conditional coverage when considering all possible instances of the source database has been proven to be an unsolvable problem.

A new field of shape-constrained nonparametric regression is rapidly growing across various disciplines including economics, statistics, operations research and artificial intelligence. Recent advancements in the analysis of productivity and efficiency now incorporate a variety of new approaches. The analysis of productivity and efficiency relies heavily on frontier models which separate relevant and irrelevant data points in various applications. The techniques applied so far have primarily been based on specific parametric or non-parametric methods but a new unified framework based on convex regression is gaining traction. The absence of commercial software for these methods has hinderly their practical application. The development of pyStoNED aims to bridge this gap by providing a python library with the capability to handle and compare different methods in the context of productivity and efficiency analysis. The library offers a range of tools and functions for data visualization, sensitivity analysis and frontier estimation based on the combination of the techniques of Lasso, DarkHorse and Gower, each suited to different data sets. The case study of US agriculture displays the effectiveness of this combination in the real world. The methodology is the first to implement a model-free cross-efficient approach using convex regression and demonstrates its practical application in the analysis of the productivity of US agriculture.

This research explores an efficient method for determining the unknown coupling between the Standard Model's Higgs boson and top quarks, using data from two-source interactions at the Large Hadron Collider. New physics is searched for beyond the Standard Model, particularly in interactions between the Higgs boson and top quarks that result in two jets, two leptons, and an undetected object. With the aid of a truth-based model and simulation of various detector factors, analysis markers are developed to identify these processes. Notably, this study demonstrates how an earlier, simpler analysis affected the measurement of the Higgs boson's coupling and the associated statistical error. With the increased luminosity of the LHC in its second phase, the model predicts that LHC Run 2 data can provide a precise measurement equivalent to 40.7, 43.5, and 99.9 percent confidence that the Higgs top coupling is within its expected standard value, for $\phi$ coupling multipliers of 1, 0.9, and 1.1 respectively. Furthermore, the model predicts new physics existence with confidence levels of 68.7, 95.6, and 99.9 percent, for $\phi$ coupling multipliers of 1, 0.9, and 1.1 respectively, and new phase factors ($\tan \alpha$) of 0.5, 0.9, and 1.5 respectively.

Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituent parsing models, UPOA and its enhanced version UPIO, both of which use the syntactic distance from self-attention weight matrices in pre-trained language models to evaluate sentence structures. Further experiments were conducted by fine-tuning the inner MLPMixer layer of the model to yield the best results. The resulting models outperformed their predecessors in unsupervised and few-shot parsing exercises.

Our research demonstrates the feasibility of combining Kaldi's advanced speech
recognition technology with Deutsche Telekom's research platform. We present a
streamlined implementation of Kaldi's German recognition model and evaluate
its performance using various German speech corpora. The findings also examine
the impact of pronunciation variations on speech recognition accuracy within
the Deutsche Telekom corpus. Furthermore, a comparative assessment is
conducting to gauge the effectiveness of Kaldi's models compared to state-of-the-art
models developed by other institutions.

The origin of Be-type stars is still unclear with theories involving both single and dual star evolutions, however through 73 VFTS spectra analyses it has been observed that Be-type stars have higher rotational speeds. Calculations reveal that their projected rotation speeds cannot all be at critical velocity, instead they range between 320 to 350 km/s. These Be-type stars have slower than expected rotation and there are fewer than expected stars with rotation speeds below 40% of critical velocity. In comparison to normal B-type stars, there are fewer Be-type stars with rapid rotation and even lower rates of being in binary systems with smaller radial amplitudes. These patterns are similar in a sample from the Small Magellanic Cloud and a direct from the Large Magellanic Cloud, suggesting a distinct characteristic of Be-type stars. These findings are in better agreement with models of two-star co-evolution than with single-star spin evolution models.

To translate ASR output into written text, inverse text normalization is utilized.
Existing ITN techniques, whether rule-based or neural modeling approaches, often
involve complicated annotations and data preparation, including the need for costly,
domain-specific, high-quality training examples. In contrast, our proposed data
enhancement technique efficiently creates large amounts of accurate spoken-written
pairs from unrelated texts with minimal manual annotation. Furthermore, our
technique's effectiveness has been experimentally validated by significantly
outperforming traditional methods in various numerical formats such as integers,
currency values, and fractional numbers with a substantial accuracy boost of 14.44%.

This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing 
that the optimal configuration is a half-space, and investigates the conditions 
under which equality occurs.

Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical areas like medical imaging. A promising approach, kernel methods, offers a more transparent and mathematically clearer framework for classification. However, incorporating kernel methods in real-world applications is challenging due to their large computational and memory demands. To overcome this issue, we develop a new method that employs non-uniform sampling and sparse tangent kernel representation, significantly reducing computational and memory costs without sacrificing accuracy. This technique enables the efficient use of kernel methods in large-scale deep neural network training for the first time.

Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant gap in the field. In this study, we take a general approach to investigating one-dimensional non-Hermitian topological systems with and without correlations. Our findings show that correlations significantly reduce topological characteristics, eliminating the extended non-Hermitian gaps even if the uncorrelated system features multiple band gaps. We derived two distinct types of topological transitions triggered by correlations, referred to as correlations-induced ideal and pseudo-gaps. Our analysis includes an exploration of pseudo-gaps, which emerge from transitions at imaginary part thresholds and give rise to exceptional points with symmetrical, positive-mass properties. We also identify the necessary conditions for pseudo-gaps and ideal gaps, establish methods for distinguishing between gapped and gapless systems even in the presence of correlations, and explore pseudo-gaps and ideal gaps in terms of fermionic quasi-particle spectra and electron transmission functions. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of one-dimensional topological systems with correlations and sheds new light on the structure of correlations.

Our current research builds upon our earlier findings where we identified acoustic characteristics essential to synthetic speech perception as warm and competent. We now aim to explore how these derived acoustic features contribute to their understanding as social entities. We have developed a two-step model for representing the association between these acoustic characteristics and the desired social attributes, using multiple supervised learning methods, such as regularized logistic regression and neural networks. The outcomes show that our approach is effective in capturing the intricate relationships between these acoustic features and the resulting social speech properties. Furthermore, the obtained models are achievable and can be implemented in the synthesis of practical spoken language systems.

A radiative seesaw model incorporating light dark matter and featuring modular A4 and gauged U(1)_(B-L) symmetries is proposed, where neutrino masses emerge through one-loop and tree-level processes. Utilizing the modular symmetry, we explore the numerical range of the neutrino mixing angle theta_13 and relate it to the light dark matter's interaction rate, which is measured by the direct detection experiment XMASS. As a result, we obtain a constraint on the model's parameter space based on the mixing angle theta13 and dark matter mass m_X. Furthermore, we investigate how neutrino oscillation data may yield information about future jet energy loss measurements in heavy ion collisions.

Building on the Heisenberg algebra concept of minimal length, a new geometrical approach to the Bohr-Mottelson model for nuclei is explored. By incorporating the minimal length parameter into the Hamiltonian, a general expression for collective inertia is derived. Results for low-lying quadrupole vibrations in 20Ne, 24Mg, and 28Si nuclei demonstrate the minimal length's collective implications, with collective motions tied to intrinsic properties of wave functions. Furthermore, a limit is established for the minimal length parameter based on total binding energy.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs can be formed from rings with ring identities, thereby eliminating the need for direct matrix calculations. Additionally, by utilizing four-dimensional ring identities, a method is provided to construct GCA quadruples through the selection of suitable one-dimensional subarrays. To illustrate the benefits of these constructions, numerical simulations are conducted for GCA pairs and quadruples in three-dimensional space, utilizing planar and spherical arrays. The results show that the proposed constructions can lead to significant improvements in system throughput with short packets without incurring significant signal power loss.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques, researchers address the complexities of analyzing numerous spectral bands within bi-temporal hyperspectral images. This study proposes a cutting-edge approach using a novel deep convolutional autoencoder that fuses features across hierarchical levels and receptive fields. By utilizing an unsupervised change detection technique, it overcomes the limitations of other approaches in hyperspectral image analysis. By comparing our method with existing techniques, it has been demonstrated that our approach yields more accurate results with better precision and recall rates, as evidenced by the evaluation of our method on diverse datasets.

A comprehensive study examines the connection between residual entropy and viscosity by using high-dynamic-range simulations of several molecular fluid models, including both accurate models and simplified steel and alloy models. Specifically, the research targets the S-Cube project's unique steel and alloy model classes, assessing their thermodynamic, viscous, and elastic properties across a wide temperature and frequency range. By performing molecular dynamics simulations on various binary and ternary steel and alloy systems, the study takes an inherent structure approach, which yields substantial results. Comparing the S-Cube and actual materials, the research reveals close agreements in thermodynamic properties but slight discrepancies in viscous behavior. Additionally, the study analyzes the S-Cube model's potential for scaling and evaluates several entropy models that may be useful for developing advanced materials. Finally, the research provides extensive databases of material properties, which can be utilized in other fields, such as geophysics and astrophysics, to support engineering applications in those domains.

The possibility that our Universe undergoes a periodic transformation from expansion to contraction is investigated in this study. Expanding upon a previous model developed by Fabri and Ruzmaikin, we establish a more stringent connection between the two phases by ensuring that the scale factor at the conclusion of the initial expansion is identical to the scale factor at the commencement of the second expansion phase. Consequently, the model yields a periodic version of the standard Lambda CDM model, where both expansion periods demonstrate identical Lambda CDM characteristics with respect to Hubble's constant, matter density, and the Hubble parameter. Although the model is the same in both epochs, the observed values of these parameters could potentially differ due to uncertainties in measurement or variations in space and time. Furthermore, the model is designed such that the universe could be consistently described as either periodically static or periodically oscillating using the standard Lambda CDM model, where the latter case is achieved by selecting a suitable matter density. As a result, the model is the same regardless of whether the universe is periodically static or periodically oscillating.

A new superdeterministic theory of quantum mechanics known as Invariant-set theory is being proposed. This idea brings concepts from areas like chaos theory and dynamical systems into the study of quantum foundations. Despite this potential, developing a clear hidden-variable model for it has been a challenge, making it hard to properly evaluate. In this piece, we create a hidden-variable model for the theory and use it to resolve the puzzle of quantum predictions from a single measurement. We also identify issues within the theory, such as the existence of numerous possible hidden values, the lack of a clear explanation of why some outcomes are more probable than others, and the failure of the theory to accurately predict the no-go theorem for relevance. The models presented here reveal that superdeterministic theories of quantum mechanics that explain relevance relations may not be consistent with the requirements of such theories.

We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on devices such as smart speakers and wearables. Our focus is on executing NN inference inside NN processors, specifically the Google Edge TPU and the NVIDIA Jetson Nano. Firstly, we evaluate if NN processing is feasible for low-power devices. Next, we analyze how to optimize the non-linearity of NN neurons using thresholding techniques to minimize computation requirements. Additionally, we investigate if reducing the precision of computed values can save power without affecting accuracy. Lastly, we check if the accuracy of classifying a custom set of keywords, known as Wordspotting Vocabulary (WSV), can serve as an adequate proxy for NN accuracy in general.

In the case where lattice spacing vanishes, the analysis focuses on the dimer model on isoradial graphs in the presence of $SL(N,\mathbb{C})$ gauge fields with zero curl except at specified punctures. The cluster expansion of the partition function for the twisted dimer model is matched with the analogous cluster expansion of the 2D Dirac partition function within this gauge field scenario, also referred to as the tau function. This derivation validates earlier proposed conjectures that relate isoradial dimer models to 2D Dirac fermions in curved background gauge fields. The method employed incorporates the use of Ryshik's reformulation of the Weyl algebra and the use of the Lax representation for difference equations.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. We introduce a new technique to improve Group Lasso estimates for high-dimensional categorical data, building upon an initial investigation into correcting bias through simple adjustment of the estimated parameters. Our method utilizes an empirical distribution of categorical probabilities to rectify the bias, producing corrected estimates that maintain sparse modeling while improving accuracy. Through theoretical analysis and Monte Carlo simulations, we examine the performance of our approach, comparing it to state-of-the-art methods on both simulated and real-world data.

Embedding high-intensity workloads and safeguarding of safety-critical processes within the same host system is becoming increasingly common, particularly in systems with mixed-criticality capabilities, such as embedded systems, automotive infotainment and control systems, and industrial automation networks. Securing the host's integrity by segregating embedded systems is a top priority, a goal that can be achieved by providing embedded virtualization capabilities. Hypervisors play a crucial role in this process, abstracing virtual hardware, including execution resources, I/O devices, and memory, while connecting virtualized devices to the physical hardware. This research aims to develop a set of virtualized hardware resources for embedded hypervisors by creating a generic model that leverages the capabilities of virtualization technology. Furthermore, a prototype hypervisor, dubbed T-Visor, is presented and compared with the existing EMU-Visor hypervisor, showcasing the potential of this technology. Experimental results indicate that the proposed T-Visor prototype exhibits a timely response to process demands, while its performance compares favorably to that of EMU-Visor.

Creating a comprehensive perspective with multiple images poses significant challenges, mainly caused by discrepancies in perspective. The issue has been addressed using perspective-corrected stitching, yet most solutions rely on approximate estimates of the exact orientation of images. Notably, humans are able to achieve remarkable results by referencing environmental cues, including the influence of gravity. This paper presents an innovative approach to full-view image merging, capitalizing on prior knowledge of objects oriented along the ground to achieve seamless results. It formulates perspective-corrected registration as a optimization problem, incorporating the perspective-corrected stitchability score to minimize discrepancies in image perspective. Furthermore, this method eliminates the need for approximate initial estimates, achieving global optimization. The experimentally demonstrated outcomes demonstrate that this method yields exceptional results with minimal input, matching the quality of state-of-the-art techniques, while requiring significantly fewer parameters.

When two identical populations of oscillators with uniform synchronization properties are connected in a loop, even with external drives turned off, the populations will enter a synchronized yet distinct asynchronous state known as a chimeric pattern. This document provides mathematical equations describing this phenomenon, and numerical analyses are performed to examine how varying parameters affect this pattern. Interestingly, increasing the heterogeneity within these populations shifts the equilibrium from complete synchronization to the chimeric state. Furthermore, manipulating the coupling strength or external drive frequency can switch the chimeric pattern between different states. This research, which is validated using numerical simulations of coupled van der Pol oscillators, offers a new perspective on the properties of chimeras even when there is random disorder within these systems.

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust in unanticipated scenarios. Building upon a recent study by Kang et al. \cite{Kang2021}, which linked the robustness of these controllers with their uncertainty's posterior contraction, we investigate the robustness of Reinforcement Learning controllers. Our work first extends the existing results to cover more scenarios, and then provides a framework for boosting the robustness of these controllers by boosting the concentration rate of their model estimations. Our proposed methodology, which is based on the Cone-Concentration inequality for Kernel Regression, achieves this. Through simulated experiments on a pendulum-like system, we evaluate the efficacy of this method, which outcomes demonstrate the satisfaction of the robustness requirements.

We present a multi-layer quiver in this paper, using which we can build a higher dimension (n+1) algebras of infinite complexity from a given n-dimensional algebra. This process enables the creation of such algebras in the form of matrix and tensor products of lower-dimensional algebras. Consequently, it results in the equivalence of category between CHT functors of certain multi-layer quivers and matrix and tensor products of quivers for the respective dimensions.

Research in holographic theories reveals a duality between reflected entropy and entanglement wedge cross-sectional area.  Building upon this concept, a similar duality is demonstrated using random tensor networks.  By examining individual tensors, non-trivial effects are discovered that resolve discrepancies at the page phase transition.  By aggregating these effects, the reflected entanglement spectrum in random tensor networks is derived.  It converges to the expected holographic result for large system sizes, yet accurately reproduces the entanglement spectrum across all system sizes, including the page phase transition.  This consensus achieved through tensor network methods aligns with holographic insights, while also enhancing our understanding of random tensor networks.

Complex systems' understanding has long been shaped by the intersection of nature and man-made aspects, with analogies to living systems often serving as key drivers. A core distinction between approaches arises from how one approaches representation vs. discovery - whether one designs a representation to capture recurring patterns or discovers underlying, objective principles governing systems. A framework for analyzing patterns that emerge consistently, such as heritable information in stochastic dynamics, can help separate universal laws from mere emergent properties. Living systems often exhibit remarkable coherence and resilience, suggesting that this patterns-that-persist criterion could help reveal essential features of organizational principles within such systems. In this study, heritable information is explored as a measure of a system's organization and used to parse a wide range of computational simulations with varying levels of noise and complexity. The patterns that emerge through this criterion could lay the groundwork for a deeper understanding of computational processes and may reveal fundamental principles applicable to both living and non-living systems, as well as insights into the broader implications of such principles.

We investigate the dynamics of a basic 3D version of the H\'{e}non map, specifically focusing on its dissipative and orientation-preserving variants. A thorough analysis of bifurcations in this system reveals that the emergence of periodic orbits, especially at specific resonant points, leads to distinct patterns in the parameter space. The system also exhibits complex attractors such as invariant circles and chaotic motion, identifiable through rotation numbers and Lyapunov exponents. The chaotic motion includes patterns similar to those of H\'{e}non and Lorenz systems, arising either from a period-doubling sequence or from the disruption of stable circles by an external periodic force.

This paper undertakes the examination of the gravitational holonomy, expressed through the Wilson loop, by dividing the spatial area over which the gravitational field gauge is imposed according to ADM variables conditions. In the paper, the source of confusion surrounding the definition of the gravitational holonomy in the literature is addressed, and a simplified method for calculating its anti-self dual component is proposed. The study demonstrates that the gravitational holonomy can be easily computed in the presence of isolated spin sources and reflects their impact on the quantum state of the gravity field, effectively encoding the information about the sources' action on the gravity field, utilizing the BV formulation and an effective quantum mechanics approach for a system with a non-trivial action. Additionally, the study highlights the relationship between the gravitational holonomy and the Wilson loop, as well as their connections to the CHS operators, emphasizing their shared role in conveying information about the gravity field sources' action, while generalized CHS operators preserve the characteristics of their original sectorators.

We analyze the statistical behavior for specific $t = 2$ or $3$, examining
the behavior of the number of hook lengths divisible by $t$ for partitions of
$n$ that fit into respective one- and two- part partitions. Ultimately,
our findings lead to new insights on the asymptotic behavior for a broader class
of $t$ and shape parameters.

Quantum particles experiencing tunneling can be studied by analyzing the Larmor clock in a weak magnetic field. The clock registers two tunneling times,  $\tau_y$ and $\tau_z$, corresponding to particles approaching a potential barrier in the $y$ or $z$ direction. There is a discrepancy between the definition of tunneling time by B{\"u}ttiker and Steinberg, with the latter identifying the actual tunneling time (ATT) as the average of $\tau_z$ and the Larmor frequency $f_L$ penalized for excessive arrival times. Research on tunneling time in quantum particles has been ongoing, with recent studies suggesting that ATT is the correct measure for particles like electrons and photons. However, there's still disagreement over the fact that ATT can be infinite, and that $\tau_z$ alone is a more reliable indicator of the tunneling process. Our study focuses on the ATT by examining its relationship to spin fluctuations in particles with spin-$1/2$, where the time it takes to lose coherence is directly linked to the ATT. Theoretical predictions indicate that ATT can be as short as the Heisenberg uncertainty principle suggests, by combing $\tau_z$ and $f_L$. The study reveals that as the particle's spin becomes more certain, the ATT increases, indicating that for an accurate assessment, $\tau_z$ should be considered in conjunction with other factors.

This research investigates the leading twist distribution amplitudes of P-wave non-relativistic mesons, demonstrating that at a leading order approximation, these amplitudes can be represented by a single, universal function, irrespective of specific meson types. As an example, the amplitudes for P-wave charmonia mesons are studied, utilizing QCD sum rules to establish a model for the universal function specific to this meson type. Moreover, the research establishes connections between the moments of the universal function and the matrix elements controlling non-relativistic corrections in P-wave charmonia amplitudes. Our findings yield constraints on the leading twist distribution amplitudes of other P-wave mesons.

Researchers have suggested the application of quantum interferometry and information processing in Bose-Einstein condensates. However, the current understanding of BECs relies on complex descriptions, often through quantum field theory or nonlinear differential equations. These descriptions sometimes conflict with key principles in interferometry and information processing. Nevertheless, a possibility of compatibility remains, and we provide a solid foundation for quantum operations, derived from solving evolution equations, and build upon this base with control techniques and efficient state sampling methods to develop practical nonlinear gates, especially a nonlinear Hadamard gate. Furthermore, our work in BEC interferometry and quantum computing redefines the paradigm by incorporating principles from nonlinear quantum mechanics, effectively applying it to interferometry and information processing.

The extended BMS algebra generated by supertranslation and superrotation vector fields at null infinity is predicted to be the symmetry algebra of the quantum gravity S-matrix. However, determining the algebra of quantized extended BMS charges has proven challenging. Recent advancements in celestial holography indicate a closed symmetry algebra without a central extension or anomaly, whereas other research suggests that quantizing these charges results in a deformation when combined. This paper reexamines this problem considering updated understanding of superrotation charges and finds that quantization of eBMS charges within a new phase space, which includes a spin memory mode, leads to an algebra without a deformation. The degenerate vacua are characterized by the soft news and a Schwarzian mode corresponding to deformations of the celestial metric by superrotations, potentially reconciling two manifestations of asymptotic symmetries through null infinity asymptotic quantization and celestial holography.

Learning with an ever-growing number of categories poses a significant challenge.  Online machines are capable of processing each new observation one at a time, without needing to reanalyze previous data.  Unfortunately, current models either need to reprocess previous data or struggle with performance after a certain point.  This research presents a new type of neural architecture called ONLINE-OLCA, capable of adapting and integrating new observations into a robust framework with limited storage needs.  This architecture achieves this by integrating two key components - olca's compact codifications that efficiently process new data and categorized outputs - to create a cohesive whole.  This architecture has been proven to perform consistently well and requires minimal updates to existing code, and has even outperformed other methods on datasets that were previously used to evaluate models processing large datasets over long periods of time.

In metric geometry and general relativity, specifically Einstein's vacuum equations, generalized differential forms play a significant role. They involve applying Cartan's structure equations and generalizing them to explore new concepts.
