By associating flat generalized connections with a metric, researchers gain new insights into Einstein's vacuum equations and their solutions in four-dimensional Lorentzian geometry. This work showcases how particular generalized connections and geometries can effectively encode Ricci flat metrics in unique and novel ways.

In the wake of several recently constructed permutation polynomials over finite fields with odd characteristics, our focus lies on exploring further permutation polynomials of the form $(x^{q^2} + x^{q} + f(x))$ over finite fields with odd characteristics, where $f(x)$ is a polynomial of degree less than $q^2$ within the same field. The investigation of the derivative of this polynomial leads to the establishment of necessary and sufficient conditions on the coefficients of $f(x)$ for these polynomials to be permutations, using both one-to-one and surjectivity analyses. Utilizing these conditions, new permutation polynomials are derived, along with various types of complete permutation polynomials, where the latter method often employs the Chinese Remainder Theorem. Ultimately, our findings include a set of all possible degree two complete permutation polynomials over finite fields with odd characteristics, where $q$ is equal to $7$ or greater.

Approximately $4 billion people around the world are affected by intestinal parasites,
resulting in significant health issues such as nausea, abdominal pain, and even death.
The difficulties in classification and identification processes contribute significantly
to the underreporting of cases. A proposed system utilizes DBN networks to classify
parasite species from light-microscope image samples, aiming to enhance the efficiency
of manual inspections and reduce the occurrence of diseases. This system's effectiveness
is evaluated using selected images of various intestinal parasites, including hookworm,
Ascaris lumbricoides, Typhus, Strongyloides, Ascaris, Trichuris, Ankylostoma,
and T. saginata species, which were sourced from earlier studies. The dataset comprises
a total of 2100 images, divided into sets of training, validation, and testing samples.
The validation results indicate that the system classifies parasite species with an average
accuracy of 89.8% while also suggesting avenues for future enhancements.

This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models. It incorporates both proportional reinsurance and loss-overlimit reinsurance models. To calculate the Nash equilibrium, a Markov chain approximation approach and a dynamical programming technique are used to solve nonlinear integro-differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations. In addition, the research shows the convergence of the approximating sequences to the accurate solution of the value functions, which is supported by several numerical case studies.

This research presents a novel Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) control strategy, integrating a derivative filter, to enhance quadcopter stability in chaotic and unpredictable flight conditions. The mathematical framework is established based on a highly accurate model that effectively accounts for non-linearities, uncertainty, and interdependence. The integration of measurement noise and uncertainty can lead to flight instability, and our proposed controller, paired with a heuristic Genetic Filter (GF), surpasses existing control methods by significantly reducing control effort and decreasing the effect of stochastic disturbances. The evaluation is conducted using realistic scenarios mimicking natural hazards and comparing the proposed controller with state-of-the-art algorithms to demonstrate the robustness and precision of our approach.

A comprehensive examination of pion-nucleon interactions at low energy is provided,
with the intention of offering a fundamental and educational overview relevant to current
research endeavors. Key topics addressed include the application of chiral effective
field theory, the significance of the sigma term, an understanding of the qualitative nature
of low-energy phase shifts, the physics governing the $\Delta$ resonance, and isospin violation.
It is emphasized that pion-nucleon scattering at low energy is intrinsically connected to QCD through effective
field theory while the majority of experimental data is described by models based on the resonance method.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During an earlier testing phase, prototype pilot modules of the new silicon pixel detector were put through a series of evaluations. This study takes a closer look at the software and electronic data management involved in these assessments, specifically focusing on the reconstruction algorithms used to assess the efficiency and accuracy of the upgraded detector. This investigation leverages pilot modules containing Hit Pattern Plane parasites but excludes those with Hit Pattern Plane parasites that introduce biases in the efficiency and accuracy assessments. The pilot modules tested include full-length slices from the outer edges of the detector, encompassing three layers. The results from these evaluations indicate that the efficiency and accuracy of the upgraded detector meet the anticipated standards.

We analyze the characteristics of 3,097 galaxies housing active nuclei within the Hyper Suprime-Cam survey that spans an area of 430 square degrees. A machine learning-based system is employed to identify the morphological types of these galaxies. Their findings cover a long wavelength range from 0.3 to 5.2 micron and are based on multiple filters. Initial examination reveals that 33% of these galaxies exhibit some form of merger or interaction with neighboring galaxies, with approximately 15% displaying very distinct features. A significant percentage of parent galaxies - 25% - exhibit elevated bulge-to-disk ratios, indicating a low probability of merger-driven transformation. Our research suggests that merger-driven transformation is not the primary driving force behind the activation of supermassive galaxies within the centers of parent galaxies, at least when considering activation events lasting between a few billion to 13 billion years in age.

High-energy and high-momentum fluctuations occur within the nucleus due to short-range correlations. In order to understand how this corruption of a smooth nuclear background influences its distribution and movement, we investigated this issue. We discovered that the short range correlations, which have a space-like characteristic, do not significantly affect the phase space distribution of the nucleus as a whole, particularly its average momentum and spatial properties. However, the nuclear distribution with both momentum and spatial properties is altered substantially by the short range correlations. Furthermore, the amount of influence that the short range correlations have on this altered distribution depends on the cutoff momentum of the correlations as well as the energy density of the correlations at this cutoff momentum. We also found that the short range correlations introduce an effective, non-uniform density of the nucleus that is described by a modified root-mean-square (rms) radius, which is reduced as the amount of corruption of the nucleus increases. We compared this to our actual experimental measurements of the nucleus and found them to be consistent with one another.

We are studying complex scaling as an inherent property unique to complex number systems and its implications for deep complex neural networks. By considering complex scaling as complex affine transformations, we can examine various co-domain symmetries in complex neural networks, which may lead to new insights and optimizations. As a result, we find that the standard formulation of complex activations like $c\relu(c)$ often lacks co-domain symmetry, which hinders networks' generalizability and motivates projections onto the real axis to rectify this shortcoming. Moreover, we find that combining complex scaling with previous suggestions for correcting phase-induced distortions in complex datasets yields a coherent and theoretically grounded architecture with substantial generalization improvements in experiments on two complex datasets.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the saturation of gluon distribution.  When gluon distribution becomes saturated, it establishes a distinct gluon density threshold per unit rapidity per transverse area known as the saturation momentum.  This saturation momentum represents the scale at which gluons become as common as possible, and it plays a crucial role in various high-energy processes including the modification of nuclear cross sections, the suppression of correlations in parton lepton scattering, the suppression of transverse particle density distributions and particle multiplicities in the most energetic heavy ion collisions at various angles relative to the collision axis, and the scaling phenomena observed in such collisions.

A thorough study measured the abundance of twelve key metal elements within eighty-six extremely metal-poor stars residing close to the Sun, focusing on their chemical compositions derived from the analysis of high-resolution spectral data captured using the Large Binocular Telescope and its accompanying equipment. Through an examination of photon-noise, we precisely quantify the inherent abundance variations present among these elements, revealing significant intrinsic scatter across a spectrum ranging from approximately 0.04 dex (in chromium abundance) to 0.16 dex (in sodium abundance), with an average of 0.08 dex. We explored the various factors potentially contributing to these abundance variations and found a suitable representation of the data using a model that incorporated two distinct components: a normal distribution representing Gaussian measurement errors and an underlying, multivariate normal distribution representing the inherent abundance dispersion. This analysis has far-reaching implications for improving spectroscopic abundance analysis techniques and our comprehension of the initial material composition within our galaxy, particularly among populations of metal-poor and dwarf stars.

A novel machine learning approach has been developed that identifies and measures the potential impact of omitted significant predictors on predictive models. The algorithm extends the capabilities of machine learning, enabling not only predictive tasks but also robust inference and sensitivity analysis. An empirical example demonstrates its practicality, showcasing its ability to be applied in data sets containing inherent uncertainty, such as educational assessment results. Through a case study, the framework is applied using Bayesian Additive Regression Trees, which makes predictions for a subset of students with missing financial literacy scores, followed by a comparative analysis of models with and without an influential predictor. Results indicate the predictive model is stable and reliable, as demonstrated by the minimal impact on accuracy observed in both cases.

This research introduces SQUID, an open-source tool for developing and training hybrid Quantum-Classical classification algorithms. It utilizes PyTorch for the classical components, allowing for the creation of multiple quantum models that can be optimized with back-propagation. We demonstrate SQUID's capabilities by showcasing its implementation in a standard binary classification task from the widely-used MNIST dataset. Notably, we discuss how a recently proposed quantum convolutional operator can be incorporated into the quantum classifier. Additionally, we present a discussion section where we explore the potential advantages of applying feature extraction in quantum classification.

Researchers, Chen and Garay, have examined pointwise slant submanifolds in almost Hermitian manifolds. By extending the concept of slant submanifolds to semi-slant ones, this study delves into their geometry in both Sasakian and cosymplectic manifolds. Key findings indicate a limitation on semi-slant warped products in these manifolds, after which several examples are provided to illustrate counterintuitive behavior among such semi-slant warped products.

The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to develop sensitive and efficient low-energy detectors that can operate at room temperature and are minimally maintained. Such detectors could range in weight from grams to kilograms and could detect nuclear recoil events triggered by various factors including neutron scattering, CEvNS, or interactions with dark matter. Ongoing research, including existing and planned studies, is being conducted to explore the practicality of this technique for multiple applications.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high or low activity, dependent on the dimer's orientation. A phase diagram featuring different dimer states, including stationary, oscillating, and rotating, is derived through asymptotic analysis as the gradient becomes steeper. Numerical simulations reveal that the dimer's behavior can replicate the responses of both individual active particles and colloid molecules by adapting to the surrounding activity landscape.

We investigate numerically charge-neutral collective excitations in fractional quantum Hall systems, focusing on two specific Jain states, ν=2/7 and ν=2/9 near quarter filling, and the 1/4 Fermi-liquid state, where one of the collective excitations meets certain criteria defining "magnetorotons." Meanwhile, a study on another Jain state, ν=2/7, reveals a novel type of collective excitation, distinct from the usual magnetoroton, at energy level zero, which can be detected through hexagonal defect microscopy; we also demonstrate the existence of "double magnetorotons" in this system. Furthermore, related spectral sum rules are theoretically analyzed.

Epidemics on massive contact networks with millions of individuals pose significant challenges for analysis and containment due to their immense scale. However, for networks that can be segmented into groups, describing the spread of an outbreak within each subset may provide a more manageable approach. Focusing on SIS epidemics, our analysis begins with identifying the most critical assumption required for this segmentation to be accurate and meaningful. Building on a network's geometric structure, we establish a criterion for this assumption and, using it, demonstrate its relationship with other key concepts in epidemiology and clustering. Ultimately, our results provide a framework for determining the suitability of segmentation for a given network and thus facilitates the application of more targeted and efficient strategies for analyzing and controlling epidemics.

The maximum likelihood estimator used in CMB map-making provides optimal, unbiased results as long as the underlying data models are accurate, but realistic datasets often violate this assumption, leading to biased results and circular artifacts in the final maps. These artifacts are particularly noticeable in the form of 'X's surrounding strong point sources, which can be both visually disturbing and also impact parameter estimation by distorting the surrounding 'posterior covariance' as a byproduct of a maximum likelihood estimation, that is, the inverse of the (block-)circularization matrix. In the interest of the most accurate possible estimation, a simple analytical correction is applied to the geometrically distorted reconstruction area. The proposed method is universal and can be applied with the same efficiency to all types of maps without needing to reconsider the convolution function, which depends on the characteristics of the datasets in question. Furthermore, this paper provides the full analytical expression behind the geometric transformation that corrects the circular distortion associated with maximum likelihood estimates, enabling seamless use in CMB data analysis pipelines.

Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by the complexity of meaning, often leading to misunderstandings where same phrases convey different meanings. Yet, in natural teaching settings, effectiveness of language instructions typically relies on relying on the context to decipher their meaning. We explore a variant of goal-conditioned reinforcement learning that enables this form of practical application by incorporating a goal-encoding module that can distill the essence of supplementary information, such as additional natural language descriptions. Our developed module incorporates two key features - a feature extractor that uses contextual clues, along with a compacting mechanism, to effectively simplify redundant descriptions. Empirical tests conducted on a complex multi-room gridworld setting demonstrate that this approach successfully uses description examples to learn tasks by learning the relations between states and goals, thus successfully learning from ambiguous instructions.

Quantum process tomography is crucial but extremely challenging for complex quantum channels. We propose an advanced method called shadow process tomography, offering a more practical approach by estimating a quantum channel's effects on specific states and basis vectors only. This framework is highly adaptable and suitable for various channel models, as demonstrated with successful applications in scenarios involving multi-qubit channels and quantum channels with restricted access to their initial states.

We aim to derive precise bounds for the Cheeger constant using a range of geometric attributes such as area, perimeter, inradius, circumradius, minimum width and diameter. Our approach involves establishing tight inequalities among these measures specifically for planar convex bodies, along with formulating new conjectures that stem from numerical experiments.

The advent of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) holds great potential for transforming communications systems. By harnessing their adaptability and swift deployment capabilities, it becomes feasible to supply content in densely populated areas or regions lacking infrastructure. In this study, we explore a UAV model that serves a maximum number of users at various locations within a set time frame. To achieve optimal trajectory planning, we develop an optimization problem that maximizes the covered area by minimizing the UAV's flight time, subject to constraints. A novel approach utilizing the k-anonymization technique is also described, where the optimization target is modified to conceal the UAV's identity while ensuring user privacy. Simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods in maximizing the covered area or anonymizing the UAV's flights.

The low-energy electronic structure of an unbiased bilayer graphene, characterized by quadratic dispersions at two Fermi points when high-order contributions are disregarded, differs qualitatively from that of single-layer graphene. We found that this difference leads to short-range interactions that are marginally relevant. Through the use of the renormalization group to investigate the role of interactions in the theory, we identified both Fermi points as marginally stable within the renormalization group flow and showed that, at low energies, the two Fermi points develop a cone-like dispersion, indistinguishable from that in a zero-energy Dirac material, despite the lifting of degeneracy at the Fermi points. Notably, this outcome implies that the bilayer graphene is inherently stable against many-body correlations.

The conformation of surface molecules greatly affects their functions. For the nanomolecular ring Sc2TbN@C80, the conformation directly relates to the chemical composition analyzed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, a tool that also reveals structural variations due to potential phase transitions. By studying Sc2TbN@C80 adsorbed on a nickel boron substrate, researchers found through spatial resolution analysis that the molecule exhibits thermal-induced conformation changes at around 230 K. These changes result in a distinction between the Sc and Tb regions as measured by X-ray photoemission spectroscopy. In addition, the structure of Sc2TbN@C80 undergoes a phase transition similar to multi-wall carbon, occurring at a lower temperature of 230 K and completing at 270 K. These findings provide crucial evidence of the structural transformations within the molecule and are a significant discovery in the study of molecular films.

The internet of things encompasses a network of interconnected devices, which includes various non-standard gadgets like security tokens and access controls, at an energy consumption level of $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-6}$ Watts. Present encryption methods consume too much energy to be suitable for IoT devices. Consequently, this document introduces a novel lightweight encryption protocol, specifically designed to be highly secure, efficient, and resistant to attacks, making it ideal for IoT applications. The proposed algorithm outperforms existing encryption methods like AES-128 and Two-Factor Authentication in efficiency, yet offers enhanced security by limiting the attack surface and at an energy consumption level of $10^{-6}$ Watts. Furthermore, this algorithm also meets the standards of hash functions like SHA-256.

The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum phase measurement for a spin qubit, and its efficiency in measurements can be enhanced by strategically choosing the duration of phase accumulation, $\tau$. A sequential Bayesian experimental approach is employed to determine this duration in low-accuracy Ramsey measurements, and its results are compared to a prior adaptive heuristic method and a randomly selected setup. An efficient process that enables simultaneous measurement-taking and design calculations greatly minimizes the computational overhead associated with measurement time. When the precession frequency is the sole parameter being estimated, the Bayesian method exhibits significant improvements over the adaptive heuristic and random protocols, resulting in computation time savings of two and four times, respectively.

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics, focusing on distinct scales. From a geometric perspective, a multi-scale centrality is defined as a function of the network's triangle inequality excess, quantifying connectivity at various local and global scales. This measure, Gromov centrality, assigns importance based on a node's relative accessibility using a metric independent of the distance. Its capability to identify community structures and key network components, including those with complex hierarchies, is demonstrated using synthetic and real-world networks.

From a purely non-relativistic perspective, we derive the Poisson equation solution for empty space in a scenario with a rotating gravitational system, analogous to the Sun, and consider the implications of this solution for the behavior of test objects within its gravitational field. The general solution to the Poisson equation, expressed in terms of the distance r and angle θ, is shown to exhibit properties consistent with Newton's inverse square law of gravitation to the lowest order approximation. This analysis yields two significant outcomes when considered up to the second-order approximation: firstly, the observed perihelion shift of the solar planets, and secondly, an explanation for the observed increase in mean Earth-Sun distance, a finding corroborated by recent astronomical measurements, rather than indicating an unbiased increase as proposed in Einstein's theory. This inaugural part of the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation sets the stage for the discussion of its theoretical and experimental implications in the second and final paper of this series.

Sets of matrix pencils sharing the same Kronecker canonical form are classified under strict equivalence into infinite groups called bundles. Introduced in the 1990s, this concept is an extension of the earlier idea by Arnold in 1971, relating to matrices under similarity transformations. Despite substantial research on the topology of bundles of matrix pencils, some key issues remain unresolved. This study revisits basic questions from a new perspective, applying methods from projective geometry in a concise overview.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action, we establish a simple method for achieving this transformation. Our work rigorously addresses almost all examples found in the literature, using both commutative and non-commutative topological models.

Cohen-Addad, Filtser, Klein, and Le created a stochastic tree embedding method that allows us to approximate metric spaces with independent edge weights. Their method typically yields trees with a limited number of child nodes. In this work, we have modified their approach to create embeddings with simpler structures: those that conform to minor-free graphs with bounded width. Our novel bounded-width embeddings can also be applied to planar graphs and yield trees that approximate the original metric trees while maintaining a bounded degree. These planar graph embeddings are based on a new class of quasi-minimal spanning trees, defined as spanning trees that minimize the sum of their children's distances over the original metric. Our main finding shows that for any bounded-degree quasi-minimal spanning tree, the difference in path lengths between it and a minimal spanning tree is linearly related to the number of child nodes in the quasi-minimal tree. This property allows us to create a polynomial-time algorithm that finds a quasi-minimal spanning tree with a limited number of child nodes in any planar graph. Combining this with a convex programming approach, similar to the one used in our previous work, allows us to create stochastic tree embeddings that approximate planar graphs and minor-free graphs with a linearly bounded number of child nodes.

For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior of linearly stable cycles is established in a probabilistic framework. This research then extends to periodic parabolic equations and neoclassical population dynamics models with their corresponding discrete-time analogs, revealing new findings.

The potential of using noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) lies in molecular simulations, where accurately converting spin states to electronic excitation states is crucial but challenging due to limited coherence times. To overcome this, our approach modifies the VQE, employing an existing algorithm that translates qubit excitations directly, thus reducing the need for coherence. We tested our method using the hydrogen molecule and saw significant improvements, achieving a greater precision in calculating the ground state than the traditional VQE, needing fewer steps to reach convergence. Furthermore, our adaptation allowed us to utilize coils quantum hardware for simultaneous molecular calculations. We successfully obtained a ground-state overlap of 0.990 compared to numerical results, indicating that our method is a viable route to molecular simulations with current quantum devices.

A key characteristic of deep generative models is the interaction of representation, its distribution, and a neural network mapping of representation to data, which is exploited in various techniques. To tackle the challenge of training these models globally, but not individually for each data sample, a method is presented that applies a variational inference algorithm to derive parameter and representation values that maximize the model's likelihood for an entire dataset. This method, dubbed the deep generative decoder, allows for simplified computation in both batch and online settings. It has been successfully applied to the design of an autoencoder that learns realistic image textures using random latent variables. Furthermore, it has been integrated into a method for learning disentangled semantic codes by applying a variational autoencoder in an unsupervised fashion.

The discovery of a common-spectrum process in recent NANOGrav findings has led to theories suggesting it could be evidence of a primordial stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) that may help resolve the Hubble tension. We investigate whether such a SGWB could address the Hubble tension by acting as a cosmological stiff fluid, effectively easing the tension between different models. We find that a SGWB born from quantum inflation errors could possibly account for the phenomena seen in the NANOGrav data as well as the Hubble tension. Its power spectrum would be shifted towards lower frequencies due to nonlinear effects, thus aligning with NANOGrav's findings in the 3-100 Hz frequency range. Additionally, this SGWB could ease the Hubble tension by acting as a stiff fluid in the standard cosmological model or the $\Lambda$CDM model by decreasing the present value of the Hubble constant. However, a similar analysis in the case of Advanced LIGO-Virgo data (which spans from 10 Hz to 400 Hz) did not yield any positive results as the non-linear effects were not sufficient to boost the power spectrum to such high frequencies as expected within the given time frame and budget of the experiment.

Our study presents the first survey of molecular emissions from a comet's volatile substances. We analyzed comb-like spectra from Comet C/2015 ER61 using ALMA's Atacama Compact Array, a powerful radio telescope that can detect molecules with distinct spectral lines. We detected several key volatile substances, including carbon monoxide, formaldehyde, and ethylene oxide, as well as carbon monosulfide, its sulfur-isotopic counterpart DCN, and water. We observed a unique combination of emission patterns, suggesting that carbon monosulfide might not originate exclusively from the primary CO sources. It's possible that CS, the sulfur source, comes from the polar ices, while the carbon monoxide and formaldehyde come from the equatorial ices. We also analyzed the amounts of these volatile substances to see how they changed as the comet moved away from the Sun and found that they matched previous observations of other comets. Notably, the signals from the sulfur compounds weakened faster than the signals from other molecules with similar complexities.

We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within the FRW universe, analogous to a quintessence model.
We will reexamine the non-interacting case by modifying a scalar field equation 
with a complex coefficient and further investigate interacting case by employing a 
new method to determine the interaction term, later confirmed by calculating the 
decay rate for the energy density.
In addition, we will investigate whether the current universe energy density 
approaches a certain value by calculating the present value of the parameter a.
Our study's results are then compared to a quintessence model, and finally, we 
investigate the influence of the generalised model's parameter on the equation of 
state state for a variable $\nu$.
Due to the limitation of the generalised model, $\nu$ can only take positive values 
from $-2$ to $infinity$.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts, notably in mechanical engineering.  A novel algorithm, incorporating multi-objective non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II and branch-and-bound methodology, is presented for solving such problems.  This approach leverages precise bound establishment to minimize the search space, complemented by a multi-objective non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II optimization component.  The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through a computer simulation, and its efficiency is compared with traditional genetic algorithms.

We refine and reinterpret the core principles of Lie theory, specifically Lie groupoids, through the lens of internal groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Key concepts are re-expressed, including path sources and integrated $A$-paths. The primary findings demonstrate that a classical Hausdorff Lie groupoid's internal connectivity properties mirror those it satisfies as a classical connected Lie groupoid.

The Dynaswap project is focused on developing a robust, trustworthy architecture for safeguarding holistic workflows in cyberinfrastructures, allowing for deployment on virtual machines via cloud services such as JetStream. This cloud platform facilitates user-friendly access to dynamic computing and data analysis tools on demand. Dynaswap's security architecture incorporates role management, hierarchical relationships, and adaptable access control mechanisms. By integrating cutting-edge frameworks like Authentication-Authorization-Accounting and Blockchain technology, as well as advanced security features, Dynaswap provides a comprehensive protection mechanism. Currently, the Dynaswap architecture is being validated in life-science research and educational settings within the Health Informatics field.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within written text. Approximately one-third of written text conveys the sentiments of the author. Unfortunately, current neural network-based approaches for aspect-based sentiment analysis overlook the implicit aspects mentioned in the text, as they solely rely on explicit information. The underlying question for this research is whether incorporating learned representations that also capture implicit aspects leading to the same sentiment, can enhance performance on aspect-based sentiment analysis. A pre-training framework for this purpose, which also addresses the problem of making the same predictions from implicit aspects, was developed and several experiments were conducted using this auto-encoding method to pre-train the model using real-world datasets. The results show that this approach produces better results on various datasets when compared to other benchmark approaches.

We establish a method to calculate how stratified case-control sampling affects logistic regression parameters related to a binary mediator. The proposed method yields consistent estimators for the direct and indirect effects as well as the total effect in the presence of binary endpoints and a binary mediator, especially when working with large data sets. The direct effect estimation relies on the application of a weighted average likelihood ratio test, whereas the indirect effect is evaluated using an applied a stepwise logistic regression model. The total effect can then be calculated by summing these estimates, provided certain conditions are met. The methodology is validated through simulation studies and demonstrated through an analysis of data collected on HIV transmission among women from selected clinics in Uganda.

This research delves into secure communication systems for multiple users that utilize reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to compensate for hardware limitations.
We simultaneously adjust the base station's beamforming vectors and the phase shifts on the RIS to achieve the highest possible weighted minimum secrecy rate under constraints for the base station's power output and RIS element limitations.
To address this optimization challenge, we split the problem into two simpler subproblems and use the block coordinate descent approach to iteratively solve for these subproblems through different methodologies.
Two approaches are developed to resolve the subproblems. The first method converts each problem into a second order cone programming problem that can be solved directly using the CVX optimization tool.
The second approach employs the minorization-maximization algorithm, which first develops a lower-bound concave approximation of the objective function, enabling the subproblems to be restructured into simple forms with analytical solutions.
Numerical simulations confirm the advantages of the proposed method in overcoming nonrobust designs and highlight the advantages of the MM-based algorithm in terms of a smoother objective function approximation and reduced computational complexity.

We begin by defining a task for few-shot continual learning and develop a novel theory to explain how executive function works through a new type of reinforcement learning agent. This agent, known as the "FutureEVA", uses a memory of past actions and their outcomes to predict its future behavior by learning from its past experiences. The FutureEVA achieves this using a technique called contrastive value policy learning. Additionally, we show that utility maximization conflicts with our theoretical model of executive function, leading to a research question about how the two are related. To answer this question, we propose a new technique, "hindsight summary learning", which allows the FutureEVA to utilize its past experiences differently. Finally, we use the FutureEVA to create PerMoR, a new method for tackling the sampling problem in transfer learning and experimentally demonstrate its success.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These solar proximity periods occurred from 2018 to 2019 and were close enough to the sun that we could calculate the distance between the solar corona and the spacecraft's metal body based on the speed of the solar wind. In doing so, we developed recipes for determining the solar wind energy flux. Our calculations yielded an average energy flux of around 1.43 gram per square meter per day, with a maximum of 2.38 gram per square meter per day. We also noticed a positive relationship between energy flux and the temperature of the solar corona, as well as an increase in energy flux over time, which we attributed to variations in the rate at which energy is released in solar flares and other coronal changes.

In a noncommutative setting, where locally compact Hausdorff groups act on C*-algebras, we introduce the concept of a numerable principal bundle with quantum characteristics. This generalization involves defining a locally trivial G-C*-algebra as a noncommutative analog to the total space of a numerable principal bundle. By building upon the Pedersen ideal's multipliers, we transcend Gelfand-Naimark duality to create this local triviality concept. Additionally, in cases of non-anti-actions simplicity, we demonstrate a noncommutative analog to the exponential law, involving MASA's, amenable actions, and finding that endomorphisms of certain C*-algebras are isomorphic to G-C*-algebras under specific conditions.

We show that any family of maximal almost-disjoint sets can be eliminated via a specific method of adding new elements that preserves the cardinality of $P$-points. Using this finding, we establish that it is possible in a specific set of circumstances that the first uncountable ordinal is less than the least cardinality for uniformization, but the least cardinality for amalgamation is greater, resolving two problems that have been outstanding for nearly 20 years and a further issue proposed by Brendle. Furthermore, we will provide a simplified explanation for why it is consistent that $\mathfrak{u}<\mathfrak{s}$ as proven by Blass and Shelah.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior within a linearly coupled optomechanical cavity system, where one cavity is treated with $q$-deformation. Our study reveals that $q$-deformation can induce perfectly transparent optomechanical cavities by canceling out cavity reflectivity. Moreover, we find that $q$-deformation, in combination with correct parameter selection, enables the realization of enhanced optomechanical coupling without limitations from mechanical relaxation rates. Notably, this might facilitate the exploration of strong coupling regimes with smaller-sized mechanical parts. Additionally, $q$-deformation results in the appearance of two distinct optomechanical resonances, rather than a single, in optomechanical resonance conditions. This is a consequence of the blockage of tunneling routes between the mechanical parts and cavities. Our work explores the potential of $q$-deformation to address fundamental and novel problems in optomechanics.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections in a plane that aligns with the rotors' symmetry axes, resulting in R-negative states with positive parity. Furthermore, I established a connection between reflections and R-operations, relating them to specific internal changes within the rotors, which I then used to calculate and compare the electromagnetic transition strengths of these states with those of their positive scissors mode counterparts.

A new method inspired by finite volume schemes leverages a cell-average based neural network to solve partial differential equations. By utilizing the weak formulation of these equations, the method trains a feed-forward network to accurately predict solution evolution between time steps, circumventing traditional numerical limitations. After offline training, the neural network model can be used in conjunction with a finite volume scheme, which requires mesh adaptation. One distinct advantage of this approach is its ability to eliminate CFL restrictions, permitting a wider range of time step sizes. Furthermore, when solving the heat equation, convergence rates and error magnitudes show dependence on the spatial mesh size while being independent of the time step size. Moreover, the neural network model exhibits exceptional performance in simulating shock waves and rarefaction waves within nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws.

The ALICE Collaboration has finalized the upgrade of its detector, with the current phase involving testing to mark the beginning of data collection for LHC Run 3. In conjunction, studies on the experiment's future are underway, with the primary goal being to establish the ALICE Collaboration's objectives for LHC Run 3 and beyond. In the upcoming LS3 shutdown, two major upgrades are scheduled, with the first consisting of replacing the two forward detectors with the ALICE Forward Calorimeter, a design that has undergone testing, to be installed during the break. A second LS3 upgrade, set to take place in 2024, aims to enhance the experiment's time resolution by replacing the existing T0 detector with an advanced, high-precision system. In the LS3 break, plans also call for performing various technical upgrades, including the replacement of VMM by PPD for photon detection, with the existing forward detectors being dismantled upon the completion of LS3. In the LS4 break, a comprehensive upgrade to the experiment's layout is scheduled, with the existing central barrel detectors being replaced with more precise versions designed to enhance the experiment's physics capabilities, with the goal of installing these new detectors during the LS4 break. In the experiment's final year of operation, a comprehensive upgrade to the central barrel will take place, with the central detectors being replaced with a specialized apparatus designed to collect proton-proton, lead-lead, and proton-lead data in the very forward regions, with the

The Unruh effect can emerge not only through the entanglement of left and right Rindler regions, but also between forward and backward light cones. Our analysis focuses on the geometric phase arising from this time-related entanglement between the future and past, showing that it can be effectively modelled by a $\Lambda$-system. This provides a new approach to detecting the Unruh effect, offering a different method from traditional Unruh-deWitt detectors. Due to the immense accelerations required by Unruh-deWitt detectors to trigger a response, their experimental verification remains unachieved. Conversely, we showcase that a $\Lambda$-system that is static yet time-dependent in Lab frame can detect the timelike Unruh effect using today's technology.

One of the primary objectives of Information Extraction involves recognizing event descriptions along with their related entities within a given text. This task has received significant research attention, yet efforts focused on non-English languages remain largely underrepresented due to a lack of quality datasets required for model development and evaluation. To address this gap, we have developed a Multilingual Event Extraction dataset featuring detailed event annotations for over eight thousand texts spanning more than three hundred million words across twenty languages, including comprehensive annotations for both events and related entities, as well as their corresponding semantic descriptions. This dataset is distinguished by its utilization of rich semantic annotations, which have been further analyzed to illustrate the diversity of events and entities involved. Furthermore, we have designed a number of experimental and evaluation techniques aimed at assessing model performance and predicting future challenges that may arise. This dataset has been made publicly accessible at https://grl.nju.edu.cn/NMEE.

We examine a complex manifold with a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle and its flag bundles, coupled with their respective universal bundles, now endowed with the induced metrics. A crucial aspect of our research involves establishing the validity, pointwise in Chern forms, of the universal push-forward formula for all universal bundles. A fundamental consequence of this outcome is the derivation of the sign of the universal -n forms on the flag bundles of Griffiths example.

Observations from the XMM-Newton telescope revealed how a clumpy stellar wind from a companion star in high mass X-ray binaries impacts the variable absorption and timing properties of the emitted X-rays. We analyzed a 7.22 day dataset from the Cyg X-1 Hard state Observations campaign and discovered notable changes in the source's behavior during periods of strong wind and when the donor star is aligned with its companion. Enhanced wind causes an increase in soft X-ray absorption, altered Compton upscattering rates, and increased variability in hard and soft X-ray bands. The shifts can be attributed to the combination of delayed and delayed delayed Comptonization, resulting in a more pronounced and bimodal variability spectrum. The proposed model improves the understanding of wind effects, offering a potential tool for exploring black hole system properties, including the properties of the accretion flow and the donor star.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed, focusing on a finite temperature environment and its mathematical formulation within the canonical quantization framework. A novel observation arises, suggesting that thermal expansion according to the Stefan-Boltzmann law may be seen as an manifestation of a non-Abelian gauge potential's topological structure, specifically when symmetry is maintained. Additionally, implications stemming from the non-Abian nature of the gauge group are explored, yielding suggestions that thermal expansion may be localized in certain scenarios, such as within early Universe plasmas or in superdense states.

Researchers have long sought to bridge the gap between syntax and semantics parsing but so far have had to make a choice between excelling in one area with a grammar-based parser or another with a semantics-based parser. This research proposes a new approach called JESP, a joint parser that can simultaneously learn to analyze the structure and meaning of sentences, achieving high performance in both areas. JESP combines the best of parser types by using a set of predefined rules for structure and a learning model for meaning, thus yielding improvements for both. Experiments were conducted using the BEAUTIFUL dataset, a resource that comes with its analysis broken down into its different components, allowing for fair evaluation. Results show that JESP excels in both structure and semantic analysis, surpassing other similar systems.

The formation of magnetically-driven jets from a spinning black hole following a compact binary merger is a potentially significant event, capable of launching outflows that may be responsible for kilonova "blue wink" phenomena and the r-process resulting from the merger. By utilizing the MRI to produce disk instability, we have conducted 3D simulations of the postmerger phase and identified the formation of jets forming at around 11.5 ms. Prior to this event, the disk develops a "dead layer' where neutrons are not heated by the accretion process, leading to the presence of a nearly stationary magnetically-driven wind. This analysis reveals that the merger-driven jets have speeds of approximately 0.12c, similar to those observed in previous studies, while the wind has a low mass distribution, peaks at the 'dead layer' boundary, and primarily consists of nuclei. The accompanying neutron wind, though heavier than the ionized component, is negligible in terms of overall outflow mass. As such, we propose a two-component model where the inclusion of both alpha-process elements in the wind, as well as the material present in the 'dead layer', can account for the abundance of approximately 100 nuclei, whereas the neutrino-heated wind contributes a significant fraction of the material's electron-yield.

We undertook a study utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program to analyze tidal features in the outskirts of 34,71 early-type galaxies that experienced either mergers or outflows. By exploring these features across a range of redshifts for their properties and distances, we aimed to estimate the frequency of such mergers. The results revealed that the ratio of tidal force decreased with increasing distance from the center of the galaxies, consistent with predictions of outside-in galactic structure development. The observed characteristics also supported a model where the outer regions of galaxies are shaped by events of lower intensity. The incidence of tidal features within early-type galaxies of all masses that underwent mergers or outflows was found to be similar to what has been observed in less massive elliptical galaxies. The estimated merger rate for larger galaxies of interest to astronomers in this sample was significantly higher than what has been reported in previous studies. The findings suggested that galaxies with masses greater than a critical value undergo mergers with smaller galaxies at a rate that exceeds what would be predicted based on the overall density of galaxies in this mass range.

This is the second installment of a series that builds upon the previously posted paper in arXiv, specifically focusing on how the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation generates bipolar outflows that can be perceived as jet-like phenomena. The AASTGrav, as the theory is denoted, views these outflows as a manifestation of a repulsive force exerted by gravitation. The underlying concept is that an object falling towards a central point of higher mass would, if it possesses properties of uniform rotation, utilize its angular momentum to create a radial motion inhibited by the centrifugal effect. The point of maximum radial velocity would be close to the Lagrangian point L1, and a subsequent analysis involving the Schwarzschild metric would reveal the role of a repulsive force in generating observed jet-like phenomena in various celestial environments. The presentation includes accompanying graphs and illustrations.

We have gathered a vast dataset of observations during fast radio bursts (FRBs), their preceding periods, and subsequent intervals. The collected samples encompass a wide range of FRB 68T's emission profiles, spanning from rising to decay patterns, although we still require more observations for a more comprehensive understanding. By combining observations across multiple wavelengths, we aimed to identify potential precursors or counterparts to FRBs, as well as their optical counterparts. However, due to the low number of FRBs and their random occurrence, our observational results show no distinct Fraser distribution. Nevertheless, we have established the first concrete bounds for the duration of an FRB's optical emission, with a 95% confidence level spanning from $0.17$ to $2.85$ seconds. These restrictions could be relaxed further with an 8-fold increase in our dataset's size. Moreover, we have set the first concrete bounds for the rate of FRB-like events in nearby nebulae, with a 95% confidence level spanning from $0.26$ to $6.78$ events per decade. The resulting constraints could be tightened substantially with the success of CHIME FRB Follow-up.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model, which covers the full spectrum of CPA-NLO processes to provide a unified platform for modeling and optimizing these laser systems. This software is used to develop an integrated model for a national Ignition Facility, where it enables integrated modeling, optimization, and inverse design of the laser system, including its potential for wavefront correction.

Multimodal language generation capabilities of models like GPT-2 and GPT-3 can be leveraged for producing text that adheres to specific visual guidelines without necessitating direct image processing. This is achieved by utilizing images in conjunction with the image2text model, where generated text serves as a parameterization signal guiding visual interpretation. In this study, we explore whether image-based information can be seamlessly integrated into the text generation pipeline without explicit image understanding. A novel framework is introduced, where images are treated as undefined variables within the text signature, allowing these parameters to be learned by the model. Experimental results demonstrate that the parameters derived by the model possess semantic significance, thereby enhancing the quality and richness of the generated text. Moreover, we introduce a significant extension of existing multimodal pre-trained language models, where support for multiple visual modalities is added without requiring further pre-training, thereby allowing direct application to language models of similar scale and scope.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is analogous to the original RingCT, but incorporates a shorter transaction descriptor, achieved by applying the Pedersen sum formula.
Additionally, our method preserves the unique address feature and anonymous transaction semantics of the original RingCT.
Our experiment reveals that the Delegated RingCT transaction confirmation time is approximately 5.915 seconds, and transaction verification time is approximately 0.132 seconds.
In comparison, the original RingCT confirms transactions in approximately 7.068 seconds and verifies them in approximately 0.171 seconds.

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated progress in
using data to inform modeling in the physical and materials sciences, where
experimental data is now commonly available and extensive simulations are often
feasible. However, when data is incomplete or experimental processes impractical
due to factors such as sample size limitations or measurement noise, machine
learning can form collaborative teams with experimentalists and theorists to
leverage their respective strengths: data sets, measurement capabilities, and
theoretical models. By embracing this cooperative strategy, the challenges of
data deficits, resource constraints, and complex problem complexities can be
overcome, ultimately yielding more reliable and accurate predictions across
multiple disciplines in the materials and physical sciences.

This research examines the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into a $\Upsilon(nS)$
state accompanied by $\pi^+\pi^-$ particles, where $n=1,2,3$. It's assumed
$\Upsilon(10753)$ belongs to a typical bottomonium under the $4S$-$3D$ mixing
scenario. We find that these specific decay processes have relatively large
branching ratios of $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-3}$ and, notably, align with Belle's
experimental findings, validating our previous assignment of the $\Upsilon(10753)$
bottomonium to the $4S$-$3D$ mixing scheme. Further validation of this work
could be achieved through testing with Belle II experiment data.

This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train deep neural networks with quantized weights. Initially, we derive mathematical expressions for the exterior tangent and normal convex curves surrounding the constraint curve representing a given quantized function, and subsequently obtain the exact formulas for the exterior tangent and normal convex curves specifically applicable to the quantized function. Building on this discovery, we devise the convex curve sweeping algorithm to efficiently compute a search direction for each iteration. Furthermore, we develop a trust region subproblem model-based approximation using the convex curve sweeping algorithm, and incorporate a stability term that mimics backtracking line search. Finally, we enhance AskewSGD by incorporating learning rate scheduling, and demonstrate through numerical experiments that AskewSGD achieves substantial reductions in computation time and memory requirements while maintaining comparable accuracy to state-of-the-art quantized neural network training methods.

The Continuum Soft Robot project utilizes fully flexible mechanical systems to achieve robots that more closely resemble the anatomy of invertebrate creatures and flexible body parts of vertebrates. To introduce the concepts and challenges of this innovative area in robotics, we will be presenting an in-depth review of its current advancements and areas requiring further research. Within the framework of this research, we have compiled a comprehensive list of the key techniques for creating continuum soft robots and have identified the difficulties associated with them. Additionally, we have provided an overview of the approaches to planning and controlling these robots in three-dimensional space, highlighting the most influential strategies in this research area and analyzing their respective limitations and potential for further improvement.

The Jacobi group $G_J = \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ can be viewed as a subgroup of $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ acting on the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$ via standard action. We explore this group and its being metaplectic over the field of real numbers. Notably, being metaplectic involves adding an extra character to the group's structure. We deny the validity of a specific metaplectic action described by Anushashvili, while providing a complete description of the Jacobi group's structure. As an additional outcome, we prove that $G_J$ behaves linearly under Haar measure transfer when compared to its counterpart $G_J^{\ast} = SL_2(\mathbb{C}) \times \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, over the complex numbers. We further show that despite some initial expectations, $G_J$ behaves nonlinearly under Haar measure transfer when compared to its counterpart $G_J^{V}$, which results from applying Weil's transformation of $G_J^{\ast}$, over the real numbers. We develop a novel framework for computing the Haar measure on any linear group over a local field. As an important consequence, we establish a natural isomorphism between the spaces of automorphic forms for $G_J$ and $G_J^{V}$. This

Verifying facts using structured data can be difficult, necessitating a model's
understanding of both language and symbolic data representation. Recent
research's advancements in text-to-text transformer models have led to good
results in fact verification on table-based datasets, though they struggle with
complex datasets like WikiTableQA and Tenzing. To improve model performance on
these challenging datasets, we propose augmenting a transformer-based model with
decomposition, a component that breaks down verification tasks into simpler
subtasks: matching cell values and enforcing constraints. Decomposition facilitates the creation of training samples of various lengths, enhances model scale efficiency, and enhances human label quality. Our enhanced model achieves top ratings in table-based fact verification on both WikiTableQA and Tenzing, outperforming the previous best results significantly.

The state of the art in learned synthetic image generation involves generative adversarial networks. Initial breakthroughs in the field relied on unsupervised approaches, however current advancements are primarily based on labelled data, leading to increased control, flexibility, and stability in the generated images. Notably, these advances build on top of the foundational work done in unsupervised techniques. One effective technique involves conditioning the generative process on low-dimensional latent vectors. Despite their efficiency, supervised generative methods' capabilities are restricted by the accuracy of their label predictions. Integrating an unsupervised component, such as latent space conditioning, enables generative adversarial networks to accurately map labels and simultaneously leverage the benefits of unsupervised techniques. Through various experiments, it has been established that combining supervisor and unsupervised components results in superior performance over traditional approaches across classification, segmentation, and other tasks.

To perform Bayesian inference using nested sampling, certain algorithms must efficiently draw samples that fulfill the prior condition, effectively measuring the likelihood function's height of a given model. A family of algorithms called step samplers has been proposed, which gain an advantage by leveraging local information from previous samples. We investigate how different step sampler algorithms function and explore their performance by exploring the impact of different parameters. Furthermore, we assess their efficiency in various scenarios by testing them on a range of challenging multi-modal, highly constrained, and unconstrained problems. Our study examines how different sampling algorithms perform when given different prior bounds and investigates the effect of choice of prior. We also compare the performance of these algorithms when used with different prior choices in a Bayesian analysis of a Peterbobs synthetic dataset.

In fault-tolerant distance labelling, we're tasked with assigning brief descriptions to the points in a network so that knowing any three points' labels allows us to deduce the direct distance between any two of them, excluding the third. Our work proves that any weighted network with a specific layout (or in fact any network with limited separating elements) allows the assignment of brief descriptions with a certain length, that enables the inference of distances in networks with one point removed. These descriptions are further adapted to track the number of shortest paths, while providing bounds on label and counting oracle sizes.

In this theoretical study, we explore two-particle correlations in time and frequency for a Bose-Hubbard model subject to external driving and dissipation, specifically at and around the point where dissipation triggers a phase transition. We calculate a temporal two-particle correlation function and observe its shift in response to varying levels of inhomogeneity, distinguishing between oscillations in the presence and absence of dissipation. By transforming these results into the frequency domain using a Fourier transform, and accounting for any residual dissipation effects, we quantify the system's quasi-particle spectrum, identifying discrete excitations characteristic of the dissipative Bose-Hubbard model. We further demonstrate that the system's complex damping rates can be determined from the diverse peaks within this excitations spectrum. We also determine the width of these excitations and relate it to the residual dissipation of the system. We use these methods to study a situation where superfluid and normal component coexist. We apply these methods to the few-atom linear chain with nearest neighbor coupling and observe that the superfluid component is only present when there is a residual level of dissipation in the system.

For a given second-order linear elliptic equation with coefficients $A$, $\mathbf{b}$ and a parameter $\lambda$, defined within a bounded $\mathbb{R}^2$ domain $\Omega$ and satisfying specific smoothness and boundedness conditions, we establish existence and uniqueness of the weak solution in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ for the Dirichlet problem, where $2<p<\infty$, assuming that the equation also includes source and flux terms. Similar results are obtained for the corresponding dual problem under analogous conditions.

To ensure that medical imaging models produce accurate predictions, it is crucial to implement out-of-distribution detection capabilities. There are doubts whether traditional deep neural network-based methods are effective in identifying shifts in medical imaging domains. In contrast, Gaussian Processes offer a reliable method for distinguishing between in-distribution and out-of-distribution data due to their mathematical nature. Consequently, we suggest an efficient and hierarchical approach to integrate Gaussian Processes within Wasserstein-2 space, which can accurately propagate uncertainty through convolutional networks by leveraging distance-preserving operations. By replacing the conventional Gaussian Processes convolutions with these efficient operations, our model achieves performance comparable to the well-established deterministic U-Net algorithms in brain tissue-segmentation tasks while providing a theoretical guarantee for accurate out-of-distribution detection, which cannot be achieved by deep neural networks. Our proposed approach also surpasses previous Gaussian Processes-based models in both brain tissue-segmentation and out-of-distribution detection on medical images and chest X-Ray experiments.

Quantum systems exhibit remarkable properties when driven periodically by an external force, leading to the disappearance of thermal equilibrium. Our research focuses on how heat-induced phenomena arise in a quantum simulation of an externally-driven, trapped gas consisting of bosons, where the thermal effects are triggered and controlled by adjusting the drive strength. Using a quasi-thermal distribution, we simulate the process and observe the birth of a condensate in a peculiar mode of vibration. Our results show that this condensate originates from an abnormal vibration state characterized by weak connections with the surrounding environment. Conversely, regular modes of vibration show a strong link with the environment and thus remain at a superposition of coherent states, preventing the formation of a condensate. Ultimately, this study uncovers a novel mechanism through which coherences are transferred and showcases its utility in identifying exotic, hard-to-reach states within strongly-driven quantum systems.

The article explores the convexity properties of solutions to the Monge-Ampere equation, along with their applications in complex geometry and conformal geometry. The main contribution is a strengthened version Alexandrov's theorem, applicable to nonconvex regions with a bounded right-hand side, for which the interface between the graph of the solution and a bounded above function can be expressed as a C2, plus epsilon estimate. This estimate measures the change in curvature across the graph of the solution. The results presented are achievable under the stringent condition of smoothness. Building on these findings, the article proves the Holder continuity of solutions to the Monge-Ampere equation, with a constant of uniform excellence of p/2, where p represents the exponent for a non-linear equation of the form div(g^ij*f(u)) =f'.

Counting the recurrence of periodic events allows us to measure time. Historically, developing stable and accurate timekeeping devices was a significant undertaking. We will instead examine a different class of timekeeping devices, based on random clicking mechanisms. A comprehensive statistical analysis framework is developed to evaluate the effectiveness of these devices, with a specific example being a single two-level atom driven coherently and monitored via photodetection, representing an non-repeating clock. The photodetector signal constitutes a renormalized Lévy process, with our comprehensive model providing accurate results even in scenarios where the counting process exhibits significant fluctuations, including cases near the termination time.

This research centers on Software Defined Networks (SDN) to address the challenges of traffic engineering, fault prevention, and service delivery within reliability and energy constraints. Utilizing Fog computing, we focus on optimizing distributed traffic flows to achieve real-time service delivery, failure recovery, and service delivery reliability with the assistance of a Fog-based SDN controller. Additionally, our proposal integrates an operating system module, SoftEC, into each node to monitor network energy consumption and control device activities. By incorporating reconfigurable mid-plane technologies, our proposal aims to achieve efficient energy management while maintaining real-time service delivery. Our key objectives include maintaining real-time traffic engagement, minimizing Fog-DC connections to reduce energy consumption, and optimizing traffic flow distribution to achieve robustness levels. Through comprehensive evaluation conducted in a real-world environment, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposal in achieving notable improvements in terms of distributed traffic engagement, energy efficiency, and robustness levels with significant performance benefits.

Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, minimizing distance between images in distinct classes. Various forms of pair-wise learning methods differ in the pairs they use for training, with some focusing on images within the same class, others on distinct classes, and a few on both. We analyze the impact of different training objectives by examining the gradients of the samples in the same class and those in distinct classes. Our analysis reveals a fundamental inequality that explains the better performance of triplet loss. This allows us to create a unified framework combining advantages from different types of pair-wise loss functions, ultimately leading to improved image search results. We also show that this new framework can be successfully applied to both compact and non-compact models. Our findings are supported by various experiments on datasets such as CIFAR, ImageNet, Cars, and Stanford Action Recognition.

In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using less complex structures than those that require hierarchical organization. A key finding shows that networks featuring reduced hierarchy have significantly weaker correlations, specifically those following power-law patterns. Building upon this discovery, we propose a framework for defining network structures through a process of iterative refinement. Furthermore, we present an efficient algorithm for transforming any tensor network to one that satisfies these constraints, which can be viewed as an instance of a hyper-invariant multiplexing principle applied to quantum states. This concept is closely related to quantum error-correcting codes that span the entire holographic spectrum, which in turn inspires an efficient method for computing the entanglement entropy of complex states. This approach is capable of producing accurate results for various systems, which we demonstrate through concrete examples. This framework offers a practical tool for designing tensor networks that efficiently model highly correlated states due to their reduced computational complexity.

Our study of magnetized radio filaments at the center of the galaxy involves
overlapping local cosmic ray streams, drawing parallels to the solar zonal
magnetism phenomenon. Researchers have developed theories on how these streams
form within the local interstellar medium, and their association with the
filaments' orientation. Since these streams operate on different timescales, we
examined whether the population statistics of radio filaments could distinguish
between pre-existing and post-formation filament structure. To achieve this,
we utilized a simulation of filament formation and compared it to observations,
focusing on the distance between radio filaments between 195 and 600 parsecs.
The average separation in our simulation matches the observed value of approximately
4.6 degrees, occurring when one-stream-inflation models align and populate
the same average separation value as shock inflation. The standard deviation
also aligns with the observed value of approximately 1.5 degrees. These results
validate that the observed population spacing comes from inflating gas pockets
by cosmic ray streams for a period of roughly 1 million years before the
filaments form, which aligns with the estimated ages of the galaxy center
filaments.

A proposed paper suggests a new method of distributed conservation voltage reduction within unbalanced three-phase distribution systems, taking into consideration the inherent non-linear relationships between voltage levels and energy consumption at the distribution level. The researchers expanded existing CVR models by accounting for distribution line inductances, resulting in reduced energy savings at lower voltage levels, aligning with energy consumption patterns across various voltage levels. A centralized optimization framework utilizing a constrained AC power flow is offered to identify the optimal scheduling of distribution voltage regulators; to achieve decentralized decision-making, a communication-intensive method of local optimization via the BFGS algorithm is provided for feeder sections. Both simulated and real-world feeders are utilized to demonstrate the effectiveness and practicality of the approach.

We investigate non-stochastic bandits and experts in a delayed context, where delays are contingent upon both the time and arm choice. While delayed experts can achieve a regret of $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ even with one arm, for bandits choosing between two arms that have a known probability distribution, a regret of $\Omega(T)$ can be achieved under certain arm-dependent delay conditions. Furthermore, we present a polynomial-time algorithm known as REGER (probabilistic Expectated Regret minimizaTion), which can yield a regret of \sqrt{T} even in scenarios with small delay distributions and limited distinct delay values. The analysis of this algorithm's performance is based on a new bound that relates expected and regret losses, which may be of independent interest. The bound is applied to the case where both arms are chosen without knowledge of their distributions, resulting in a regret of \sqrt{T} as well. Notably, no algorithm is currently known to achieve this level of regret when run in the setting of delayed experts with multiple arms.

Current text-generation algorithms in dialogue can be flawed. Primarily, they tend
to produce safer, more conventional responses even though they may not fully
comprehend the question. To address this limitation, our proposed method aims to
generate more original and creative responses. The core idea is to incorporate
human-like linguistic structures and ideas in the output. To achieve this, our
system incorporates several elements: Firstly, it breaks down the input into its
components using natural language processing techniques. Secondly, it encourages
originality in the generated text by replacing certain parts with alternative
phrases. Lastly, our system learns to incorporate varied levels of abstract
thinking to ensure a richer understanding of dialogue prompts. The results of
our experiments confirm that our approach effectively increases creativity in
dialogue responses without compromising their accuracy.
