The system's effectiveness was demonstrated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for further research.

Research into two-dimensional arrays with favorable two-dimensional correlation properties has gained significant interest due to the rapid advancements in remote sensing, imaging, and wireless communication technologies. These applications require short pulse durations and minimal interference between adjacent array elements. A novel inter-group complementary code set and two-dimensional Z-complementary array code set are proposed in this paper, based on multivariable functions with multiple variable selections. These codes demonstrate the ability to function within complex systems while minimizing collisions between different code sets. By carefully choosing the variable selection criteria, the resulting codes can maintain a balanced ratio of length to diameter, thus ensuring satisfactory two-dimensional correlation properties. Various properties of the proposed code sets are theoretically proven, verified, and illustrated through practical examples.

Computed Tomography (CT) is a crucial imaging technique that provides a wide range of vital information about the human body. By utilizing multiple energy X-ray sources, CT has the ability to distinguish between different materials based on their attenuation rates, which are specific to each material and related to the material's atomic number. This makes it possible to not only reconstruct images from the acquired polyenergetic data, but also to accurately distinguish between various materials based on their relative attenuation rates. Unfortunately, the process of selecting the optimal keV level for a specific task is time-consuming and highly labor intensive. In order to overcome this limitation, the use of a versatile and advanced image reconstruction model that can not only reconstruct high-quality images, but also automatically select the optimal keV value, is proposed. This model achieves this by making use of a unique set of variables that can move freely across the multi-keV domain. This concept is further developed by creating a system of variably weighted images that are attuned to different tasks. The model is tested on a small dataset, which provides information on materials such as wood, bone and metal. The results show that the model can effectively determine the optimal keV value for a range of tasks from physics-inspired material decomposition to image denoising and reconstructions. This study confirms that the model is capable of performing well across a wide array of tasks in the field of polyenergetic CT.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate predictions for the scenarios in which the electron gap becomes very narrow, including the limit where the gap size approaches zero. Notably, if only one of these factors is considered, the model's accuracy is less precise, but surprisingly, in the context of graphene bridges, the largest discrepancy compared to the multi-factor model is minimal, less than 0.1 percent. This highlights the importance of accounting for both electron spillover and nonlocal behavior when modeling and analyzing graphene bridges.

In this research, we investigate the user's part in Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER), revealing (1) that humans outperform automated methods in pinpointing context-sensitive terms, and (2) that users can effectively utilize these tags to locate relevant entities, and (3) that enhancing visibility of supporting documents alongside a query's context improves the user's efficiency in CNER. The findings from this research may inspire future research in other Information Retrieval domains.

Time-based and multivariate data are often represented with intricate, long-term patterns. Popular tools like Plots[DateRange] in Julia and seaborn in Python can produce visually appealing results, but these results are typically static. While some studies use interactive visualizations to compare data points over time, this potential has not been fully utilized. We will share our experiences with enhancing multivariate time series and longitudinal data analysis through interactivity, presenting three key techniques: linking, brushing, and splines. These methods allow users to: 1) highlight segments on multiple plots, 2) connect related data points across different variables, and 3) analyze how different values change over time. By applying splines to handle gaps in data, users can seamlessly link segments and uncover hidden patterns. We will demonstrate these techniques using Julia and the Correlation matrix example, but the presented ideas are generally applicable, as most data visualization tasks revolve around the effective use of time and data variables, and interactive visualization is a fundamental concept that can be applied to any programming language.

The promising potential of extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a significant area of study, as machine learning models can assist healthcare professionals in decision-making to enhance overall healthcare quality. However, due to the diverse formats of EHRs, as well as the limited availability and accessibility of such data, developing effective models has become a substantial challenge. To address this, a novel framework called HSGNN has been proposed, which incorporates a heterogeneous similarity model to compactly map similar clinical objects together in the multidimensional representation space. This enables a graph neural network model to learn node representations, which in turn enables a clinical relationship understanding between nodes. As a result, a holistic picture of EHRs can be achieved through the integration of individual object representations. Extensive experiments have been conducted on real-world datasets, which demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework.

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects, we model the behavior of the electric double layer at the boundary of a charged flexible material. From a free energy model, we calculate the electrostatic potential and number of water and ions within the boundary using coupled differential equations, including Poisson's equation. We discover that solvent effects profoundly impact the electrostatic potential, ion counts, and permittivity of the electrolyte near the boundary of the charged flexible material. Furthermore, we find that taking solvent effects into account intensifies the Donnan potential and demonstrates that within the boundary of fixed charge, ion counts decrease slightly. Additionally, we find that increased ionic size strengthens the solvent effect on electrostatic properties at the boundary of the charged flexible material. Lastly, we find that high surface charge density results in decreased permittivity and water dipole counts due to solvent effects.

Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers. To this end, we annotated a unique dataset, PURE, and derived a new one combining requirements with general text. We employed multiple approaches to label the data and compared different models, including transfer learning, batch and online learning, as well as under-sampling and ensemble methods, to evaluate the generalizability of different approaches to requirement extraction. We ultimately achieved the best results with the batch undersampling method, yielding an F1-score of 0.963 on the test set, and found that fine-tuning BERT produced a modest improvement over not using BERT at all.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a maximum diversity network coding technique. A direct link between physical layer performance and the efficiency of network coding is established through the analysis of output interference and signal quality. Based on this connection, an optimization problem is formulated to find the best relay assignment and power allocation strategies, thus minimizing energy consumption while meeting quality requirements. By redefining the problem into a series of independent linear max-min problems and applying the successive approximation method, a near-optimal solution is obtained. Simulation results show that the proposed scheme yields significant gains in energy efficiency compared to traditional schemes.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local density of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting and spin-polarization patterns was achieved. However, the simulations revealed that an idealized model of two aligned exchange fields is insufficient for describing the magnetic behavior of the studied ferromagnetic high-spin dimer. For the analyzed non-magnetic YSR states, the calculated exchange fields were determined and the respective magnetic coupling constants of the dimers quantified. Based on the analysis, the proposed antiferromagnetic exchange constant for the dimer was found to be a strong, high-temperature coupling with a magnitude similar to that of the van der Waals coupling between Mn and Nb atoms.

Techniques such as distribution-to-distribution pointcloud registration have been utilized for aligning pointclouds without requiring pre-existing pointclouds. Instead, they rely on probabilistic approaches that need only one example pointcloud for initialization. A significant advantage of these methods is their ability to handle significant pointcloud changes during the processing pipeline. A major drawback, however, is the preservation error which leads to inaccurate alignment results. Research has shown that leveraging pre-trained networks for noise reduction effectively mitigates this error. Nonetheless, our approach goes a step further as it explicitly identifies and removes bias error, thus yielding more accurate alignments by combining the bias estimate with Rababah's noise-reduction technique. Furthermore, we developed a residual neural network filter to minimize bias error, and our results indicate that this method outperforms previous noise-reduction methods when evaluating the alignment of two pointclouds based on the Chamfer Distance metric.

Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in immense 
databases requiring extensive computational power for processing. Deep 
learning methods have recently gained traction for analyzing satellite images. 
Although incredibly efficient, they have inherent limitations, necessitating 
specialized computing infrastructure and large volumes of annotated data. In 
the context of massive satellite datasets, securing sufficient computational 
resources and annotated data can become financially and logistically burdensome.

We present a simplified computational model of electronic states across multiple energy levels for outer shell absorbers in materials. This multi-level rate model incorporates Auger decay, ultrasoft x-ray flux, and compares favorably with detailed simulations using the BESSR2 code. We find that outer shell state occupancies are initially increased by soft x-ray preirradiation before being reduced by high-fluence ultrasoft irradiation, ultimately leading to state depopulation and material damage. This outer shell state occupancy approach offers a readily applicable means to evaluate changes in x-ray absorption near edges and evaluate material degradation over multiple orders of magnitude.

The method for training a modulations classification neural network known as Mixture Maximum Likelihood (MML) has been developed to improve the network's resistance to attacks. This is because the traditional method of training these networks, based on a discriminative model, suffers from weaknesses that can be exploited by adversarial examples. In response, a new training method called MML-GAN was proposed, which uses an adversarial network to create data that is then used in a discriminative model. However, this approach has its own limitation as the generated data only consists of a single class and therefore may not adequately serve its purpose in improving the robustness of a discriminative model. This issue has since been addressed with the introduction of a new extension to MML-GAN, different classes with varying levels of confidence are mixed together and used to train the model, while also ensuring that the generative and discriminative models are matched. This approach has been found to provide robustness against adversarial attacks, while the source code for the paper can be found at: https://github.com/fengnie/MML-GAN_MC.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue where sequential segmentation tasks could aid segmentation performance by leveraging previous experiences. We investigated this approach through a study called "MIRU'' where four hospitals collaborated on a task: initial training using data from three hospitals and subsequent segregation using a single hospital's data, comparing it to training from scratch with the single hospital's data. The study found that training with successive experiences, or "learning continually'', did not enhance segmentation performance significantly when using large datasets. Conversely, learning continually was beneficial when working with small training sets. Ultimately, the research confirmed the hypothesis that training with successive experiences improves the segmentation process when resources are limited.

A type of comparison called bipolar comparison is presented, allowing the comparison of elements from different sets, such as sets of real numbers, vectors, or non-commutative algebras, while enabling relationships like inequalities and equalities to be interpreted in a transitive manner. The concept of a comparative structure is introduced to formalize the underlying framework for these comparisons. The comparison is utilized to establish inequalities and identities for exponential functions, trigonometric functions, vector norms, matrix norms, non-commutative algebras, and operator algebras. The study of bipolar comparisons serves as a theoretical foundation for comparing different types of variables within data science applications.

Across various disciplines, there's considerable interest in creating predictive models for complex systems using data. To tackle this, we've developed an integrated framework that combines data-driven learning and domain knowledge to identify and quantify errors in dynamical models. Our approach involves two key steps: initially, we employ machine learning techniques to construct a model from available data, which may not necessarily adhere to existing knowledge. This allows us to pinpoint potential issues in the resulting models. Subsequently, we utilize a two-step optimization process to refine the models, where we alternate between updating the state and parameter spaces to minimize discrepancies. This results in a dynamic system whose behavior closely resembles the input data, consistent with fundamental principles. We've tested our method on mock systems as well as a renowned model in climate science, demonstrating its effectiveness. To facilitate future applications, we've contributed new open-source code to the PaStA library.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, most of which are powered by young or intermediate-mass stars. This disparity appears more pronounced than in the Taurus molecular cloud. A proposed explanation for the disparity is that the difference in core properties lies in their mass distribution, with the Dragon cloud hosting larger-mass cores. Our observation of the difference in core properties without a change in their density or temperature suggests that core mass may be a key factor. This discovery implies the existence of a mechanism allowing cores to accumulate mass and is a crucial step in the development of massive star formation. Moreover, this process could also contribute to the formation of neutron stars. Consequently, it would be beneficial for future research to investigate cores in other star-forming regions, with the goal of fully understanding how massive star formation evolves.

The theoretical primordial black holes that form in the early universe are proposed as a possible explanation for dark matter. If scientists can observe the effects of these black holes on the movements of stars in the galaxy, it to predict the characteristics of various stellar streams. We have created a simulation tool, PopSyCLE, which uses the stellar N-body problem to study the dynamics of these stellar streams. We used PopSyCLE to model different scenarios of primordial black holes affecting stellar streams and examined the accuracy of several astrophysical models. Our results provide a framework for distinguishing between the effects of primordial black holes and other astrophysical phenomena that cause disruptions in stellar streams.

In a system consisting of hard wedge-shaped molecules composed of three spheres and having an asymmetrical, triangular shape with an oblique angle less than 180 degrees, the phase structure is studied as a function of the molecular shape and size disparity. The non-modulated, uniform, and ordered hexagonal phases that exist in these systems have been well-documented. In this work, the existence of two unique modulated phases with high and low frequency modulation are studied using Monte Carlo methods. The results show that these modulated phases exhibit some similarities with the oblique and monoclinic phases observed in systems composed of rigid, three-arm molecules. The frequencies of the modulated structures correlate with the molecular structure, while their stability is influenced by the size disparity.

Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer. These updated representations can then be used for tasks such as classification. The study shows that PASTA performs comparably to plug-and-math on 4 natural language processing tasks, but requires significantly fewer updates – 77 less on average. Furthermore, we explored substituting classification token embeddings and found that simply shuffling them yields similar performance to more sophisticated optimization techniques like SGD. The code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/mghit/pasta.

This paper investigates a complex task known as multi-set preference ranking, where objects from various sets need to be combined to satisfy a user's preferences. For a given user, a set of items is preferred over another if it includes all of the user's preferred items, while also excluding any of the user's non-preferred items. The user's preferences can be modeled using a distance function that measures the similarity between any two items. The existing approaches to multi-set preference ranking rely on a non-contextual assessment, where the user's preferences are evaluated based on a fixed framework. In contrast, we present a new contextual model that takes into account the item combinations that have a higher value according to the user's distance function. The user's preferences are expressed through a conditional probability. The binary contextual preference ranking problem is formulated as P(CPR), and the results show that P(CPR) is more complex than its non-contextual counterpart, with the added advantage of allowing contextual sensitivity. An experimental analysis is also conducted using real-world data from a set addition problem experiment. The user's distance function can be learned using our proposed algorithm, which is shown to outperform a competing algorithm.

Our application of the lattice cluster theory for a comprehensive assessment of
thermodynamic properties aligns with experimental findings. Additionally, in
support of theoretical models, an effective potential reflecting the thermodynamic
interactions as the primary driver of slow dynamics is proposed. Furthermore, 
considering the primary divisor of the pair effective potential leads to the 
identification of two major components contributing to dynamic inhomogeneities, 
namely configurational and positional contributions. Moreover, in line with 
Khazaee-Moradi and Frenkel's theory, the impact of these contributions on the 
cooling rate of dynamic processes can be evaluated.

Our study focuses on the impact of childhood developmental age on the language use of individuals. To answer this question, we created a new dataset of adult language incorporating negation words and contrasted responses from adults who learned this language at different fictional ages. We discovered that cutting-edge language models like RoBERTa and BART are able to infer the age at which a person learned this language, but this ability does not always translate to a better understanding of sentences containing negation words. This suggests that these models may be able to pick up on subtle social cues, like developmental stage, within a language, but this does not necessarily mean they can effectively process individual words.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our proposed mechanism into conventional attention models by exploring different look-ahead angles. Experiments have been conducted on NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks using state-of-the-art transformer models. Findings indicate that incorporating the look-ahead attention mechanism can lead to notable improvements in translation quality, and by exploring angle ranges, we can optimize its performance.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. We'll demonstrate that curvature graph weights can be explicitly defined through a hypergeometric function and an even simpler expression that combines it with a ratio of exponential functions, all based on structural parameters of the symplectic manifold. Notably, we examine a special case involving a Kähler manifold, derived from a Calabi-Yau structure, which leads to a substantial simplification of these expressions, revealing a connection to positive integer partitions.

This research involves determining the large N limit of $O(N)$ models with non-polynomial potential functions in odd dimensional spaces, leading to a new class of interacting conformal field theories. Specifically, this results in CFTs for dimensions 3+4n where n is a positive integer. Calculations of thermal entropy are also carried out for these CFTs in various dimensions. It was discovered that in some dimensions (such as 5 and 7), the thermal entropy is proportional to the number of states in a hyperbolic lattice at a specific temperature, which was previously noted by other researchers. Conversely, the entropy of entanglement for scalar fields in these CFTs exhibits a different relationship.

Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 with the development of a universal approach for pricing Asian options based on one-dimensional Markov processes. This note applies the CTMC framework, calculating the inverse Z-transform and inverse Laplace transform separately for discretely and continuously monitored options. As a result, we achieve improved explicit Laplace transforms, surpassing a prior key discovery made by Song and Yao in 2013. Moreover, we present novel bounds for the pricing of continuously monitored Asian options. Finally, both numerical experiments and theoretical analysis demonstrate the advantages of our new method over the existing key result of Song and Yao.

The source behind the diffuse gamma-ray background is currently unknown. However, various galactic features such as star-forming and starburst galaxies, black holes, and neutrino-emitting particles are candidates to explain this phenomenon. Recent studies have suggested that clusters of galaxies might be responsible for a significant portion of the gamma-ray background due to particles produced during cosmic ray interactions with intergalactic magnetic fields. We calculated the expected diffuse gamma-ray flux from galaxies that are currently observable and those that are not, using data from the Fermi-LAT. We analyzed data in two energy ranges (above 1 GeV and 100 GeV) and found an agreement within our model, which also takes into account the potential role of secondary neutrinos. However, it does not support the hypothesis that galaxies contribute a major part of the gamma-ray background. On the other hand, the expected flux from galaxies in the local universe matches the observed gamma-ray background magnitude in the 100 GeV energy range, but not in the 1 GeV range. Our model also rules out the possibility that galaxies alone can explain the gamma-ray background at both energy ranges. Clusters of galaxies may, however, be able to account for one-third to two-thirds of the gamma-ray background at the 100 GeV energy range, and for less than one-fifth of the gamma-ray background at the 1 GeV energy range. Our current understanding of galaxy data does not support the hypothesis that clusters of galaxies can alone account

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can give heavy particles a significant boost in energy, which may then produce a distinctive signal in the cosmic microwave background radiation through the process of classical cosmological particle collisions.  In this research, we examine the prospects for detecting these features through the cusp-like characteristics and plateaus in the power spectrum caused by continuous particle emission as a result of oscillations within the cusp.  These oscillations arise from particles with zero mass that were created during the inflationary era and can be viewed as being "trapped" within the cusp.  By solving the continuum field equation for this system, we explore how to reverse-engineer the properties of an osillator system, including its frequency, amplitude, and decay rate, from an observed cusp-like profile.  Furthermore, our results accurately predict the cosmological particle collisions that lead to detectable signals in the cusp, which can be measured in the cosmic microwave background radiation.  Finally, our analysis makes it clear that detecting these cosmological particle collisions does not necessarily imply that primordial features themselves can be identified.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. To address this issue, a framework called LaViSE is proposed to enable convolutional neural networks to describe the key components of any image. This process involves assigning importance to specific image filters based on their ability to effectively capture image features, and then using these filters to represent the underlying structure of the image. This structure is represented as a set of key features that can be translated into human-language descriptions. This proposed method can automatically discover and explain image features, and the results show an improvement over existing layer-wise relevance attribution methods.

Developing a simplified microscopic model of cuprates, researchers investigate the role of phonons in one-dimensional CuO chains. Through a molecular orbital calculation of CuO clusters and subsequent tight-binding model extension, the electronic properties of the material are analyzed. The research reveals that an electronic gap can be produced in the one-dimensional system, and the associated electronic gap excitation energies align with those of phonon frequencies in cuprates. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that attractive interactions can occur across significant distances within the one-dimensional framework, and these predictions show resilience to structural defects. These findings suggest that cuprates with electronic gaps may originate from phonon-driven interactions rather than from two-dimensional copper-oxygen planes.

The ongoing Population-based HIV Impact Assessment project aims to measure national and regional progress in combating the HIV epidemic, a primary goal of UNAIDS' 90-90-90 targets. By analyzing data from high-risk countries in sub-Saharan Africa, researchers hope to gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between HIV prevalence, treatment rates, viral suppression, and other key factors, ultimately informing policy decisions and strategies to combat the epidemic.

To achieve this goal, a causal learning network was developed using an integrated approach that combines multiple methods, including a Bayesian network, a causal structural learning algorithm called RfBAYES, and constraint-based methods. By leveraging these approaches with prior knowledge and expert input, the network can identify and refine connections between key variables, including age, sex, urban-rural location, and other risk factors.

To validate the network, multiple approaches were employed, including a synthetic network, real data from a HIV assessment in Malawi, and in-depth analyses of regional differences in HIV prevalence. Through these methods, the network was shown to effectively capture the relationship between variables, highlight correlations that could inform policy decisions, and point out potential weaknesses and areas for further research.

Ultimately, the resulting network provided valuable insights into the factors driving regional disparities in HIV prevalence, suggesting that demographic and urban-rural disparities may play a key role. This has significant implications for potential interventions and could inform policy decisions to combat the spread of HIV, particularly in young women who were found to be at highest risk in this

In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ of $\beta$-Mn type, it's discovered that the transition from a metastable skyrmion lattice at room temperature to an equilibrium helical state, when triggered by magnetic fields, goes through a topological transition at specific field strengths where the skyrmion density abruptly drops. Theoretical models and experiments confirm the transition to be a first-order phase transition resulting from the stabilization of the magnetization's energy minimum at specific field strengths by the strain effects. The stability of the metastable phase and the fact that the strain effects are not extremely extreme explain why previous experiments did not observe the predicted topological melting of the skyrmion lattice. The findings provide a basis for understanding and controlling the metastable skyrmion lattice's life span in related materials.

High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models are thoroughly explored, covering key 
assumptions and their underlying rationales, significant outcomes, and example
exhibits through simple demonstrations. The theory and implementation of 
these models, focusing specifically on singular ARMA models, is examined. The 
paper prioritizes detailing model types and their underlying structure, 
rather than estimation methodologies, aiming to highlight innovative 
research avenues and applicable areas which are still underdeveloped.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others, as specific instances. This paper aims to provide a clear outline illustrating the connection between fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and solutions to the equilibrium problem that satisfy particular monotonicity and Lipschitz-type constraints.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that employs deep neural networks. These models can be viewed through an interpretative lens of Bayesian probability, ensuring predictive predictions through enhanced uncertainty representation. By incorporating this form of uncertainty into steganographic secret data, Bayesian Neural Networks offer a novel method for reversible steganography. Our proposed method has been evaluated against the current state-of-the-art solutions and surpasses them in both image quality and embedded secret data, with notable improvements of 2.46 and 3.21 dB respectively, while also achieving comparable throughput.

The debate on turbulent effects influencing magnetic activity in the Sun and stars persists. The mean-field theory provides a widely applied framework to link these effects to fundamental magnetohydrodynamics, although it's only recently become possible to test its assumptions on the influence of turbulence through direct computer simulations. The article argues that attempting to understand the Sun's and stars' magnetic activity via dynamo theory is only effective when incorporating results from high-resolution direct simulations spanning the entire turbulent spectrum. Failure to do so may necessitate re-evaluating observations and measurements of cycle characteristics and the nature of star-forming regions. Examples are provided, including the potential need to revise existing models of cyclic dynamo stability and the geodynamo.

A study has revealed molecular outflows in the central area of the galaxy NGC4945 using the ALMA. At a high resolution of ~0.3", the ALMA detected four outflows including a 12CO and 13CO (1-2) outflow, and three CO (2-1) outflows. Three outflows, detected in the east and west of the nucleus, have the same direction but opposite directions, suggesting they originate from the galaxy's mid-plane. The outflows have a wide range of velocities from -410 to 160 km/s. Two other outflows, found in the north and south of the nucleus, have different directions. The outflows may be caused by the movement of gas in the galaxy's disk. The rates of outflow for the eastern and western areas were measured at 67 and 161 solar masses per year, respectively. The outflows continue to evolve over time. The movement of gas in the galaxy's disk also influences its star formation. The galaxy's central area has a high star formation rate but the movement of gas does not affect the formation of stars. The study was conducted using the ALMA. The movement of gas in the galaxy's disk could also lead to the formation of 'z-shaped' structures but the study found no evidence for this. The study was the first to use the ALMA to study outflows and star formation in the galaxy's disk. The movement of gas in the galaxy's disk also leads

A simplified version of the original Vlasov-Maxwell equations for magnetized plasmas is provided by quasilinear theory, describing how particles interact with waves through resonant processes. The reduced model in a turbulent regime shows that the distribution of particles changes over time due to a kinetic diffusion effect, where the rate of change is influenced by the density of wave energy. The model also predicts that the density of wave energy in a given spectral space evolves according to a reaction equation, with the rate of growth dependent on the distribution of particles. A numerical approach, the conservative Galerkin method, is proposed for the quasilinear model in both momentum space and spectral space. The approach ensures the preservation of physical conservation laws, employing conservative discretizations and preserving the underlying symmetries of the continuous system. The quasi-linear diffusion coefficient and energy growth rate are conserved regardless of the discretization method used. The stability of the quasilinear model in magnetized plasmas is studied through numerical simulations at different resolutions, with simulations showing that the model exhibits similar trends as kinetic theories, such as particle acceleration in the direction of the background magnetic field in regimes of weak and strong turbulence. The results also show that the conservative Galerkin method effectively preserves the particle distribution and wave energy growth in a manner consistent with the quasilinear theory.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique with a constant stepsize for linear and nonlinear ordinary differential equations, achieving successful results. In this study, we introduce a new variable stepsize approach based on SDIMSIMs with diverse starting point and amplitude in the Nordsieck matrix, thus enabling a more flexible choice of nodes for the interpolation basis. Moreover, this method allows for a greater number of nodes to be chosen from the mesh nodes, giving rise to new and older methods. We then establish strong convergence under a Lipschitz condition and demonstrate the validity of the results using various numerical examples.

We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of a specific Lyapunov inequality in B+(X,X*), where X is a Banach space. The inequality's solutions determine the boundedness of the resolvent R(λ,A) inside and outside the left half-plane and left invertibility of T, the C0-semigroup.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a computational software and web-based tool for determining the interaction cross sections between dimuonium (true muonium) and matter, also computing corresponding form factors. With these tools, researchers can estimate whether an interaction can occur, such as muonium capture by atomic nuclei or the production of the $J/\psi$ meson in certain processes. Developed for research in physics, MuMuPy is available for free use at https://mumupy.github.io. It can be run from the website without any setup or downloaded as a self-contained application for use on remote systems.

Portfolio managers assess investment success in relation to market standards, specifically using the Standard & Poor 500 index as a benchmark. Our revised assessment combines two key measures: the portfolio's absolute value and its performance relative to that of a chosen benchmark. The traditional Merton problem, however, solely focuses on the portfolio's absolute wealth. In contrast, our proposed model encompasses both absolute and relative wealth in a comprehensive utility function. The utility functions, derived from power law equations, allow for flexibility with varying exponents to suit individual benchmarks or market scenarios. The outcome provides an explicit solution and is compared to the original Merton problem solution, with implications for the Capital Asset Pricing Model framework.

The most abundant galaxy type in the cosmos is dwarf galaxies, which exhibit distinct characteristics when compared to larger, brighter counterparts. This article centers on the physical and chemical properties of the interstellar material within dwarf galaxies containing notable quantities of gas and dust. The discussion includes the characteristics of neutral and ionized gases, the effects of dust, and initial evidence suggesting the presence of active nuclei in these galaxies. The article also considers the cosmological implications of primordial helium abundance and the similarity between local Green Pea galaxies and younger, proto-galactic systems in the early universe.

We examine the stability of fermionic quasiparticles in a fermion-boson model based on a Bethe-Salpeter equation approach. In this context, fermionic quasiparticles face disruption due to interactions with local bosons, leading to a decrease in their mass as a result of this interaction. Notably, even at low temperatures and small boson occupations, the collapse of the quasiparticle can occur, with its mass incorporating a constant component that depends on the boson occupation number. Furthermore, the quasiparticle's high-density characteristics can persist in a non-zero occupation of bosons, which has implications for occupied bosonic states and the formation of a composite fermion. Moreover, the quasiparticle's high-density features can arise in a non-zero occupation of bosons even in the absence of attractive forces between fermions and bosons. As a case study, the behavior of a polaron in a system of nearly half-filled Landau levels is analyzed, with substantially dense quasiparticles forming in this environment, despite substantial occupation of bosonic states, which has implications for the phenomenon of superfluidity in systems of ultracold fermionic atoms.

Given any finite divisors divisor of n, let's denote ${\cal S}_{n,\mathbf{d}}$ as the collection of permutations that maintain a specified invariance in their cycles, where the largest cycle's length is $\mathbf{d}_1$ and the remaining cycles' lengths sum up to $n - \mathbf{d}_1$. In this context, we establish that the groups of permutations that maintain this invariance, denoted as ${\cal S}_{n,\mathbf{d}}'$, are virtually isomorphic to the generalised Thompson groups $G_d$, particularly when $d \geq 2$. Furthermore, for the braided-permutation groups of low arity defined by Brown, we identify their isomorphic counterparts as braided-Thompson groups $G_{\mathbf{d}}$, where the arities are represented by the vector $\mathbf{d}$.

This paper demonstrates the end-to-end fine-tuning of the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. Key technical hurdles are identified that must be overcome to accomplish this goal. A comparative evaluation is presented to show the superiority of the proposed approach. Additionally, the paper highlights a previously unreported but critical design decision, which involves disabling the filter on the generated text if the RAG architecture is to be end-to-end fine-tuned. This innovation allows the end-to-end fine-tuning of RAG's text generation component, while also enabling the end-to-end fine-turing of the DPR retriever.

This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a specific logarithmic weight given by $\log\left(\frac{2k}{1-x}\right)$ over the interval $(-1,1)$ where $k>1$, and we verify a long-standing conjecture of A. Magnus regarding these coefficients, making use of the Riemann-Hilbert and steepest descent methods in an unconventional manner since no solution to the related problem near the singular point at $x=1$ exists in the current mathematical literature.

Utilizing crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to acquire top-tier human annotations proves more complicated than initially thought, influenced by several key factors, such as task instructions and annotator compensation, among others. To prevent inaccurate annotations which could mislead automatic summarization systems, we develop a multi-stage recruitment process targeting high-quality MTurk workers. By establishing a rigorous evaluation pipeline, we demonstrate the ability to exclude unskilled workers before evaluation tasks are initiated, and then collect accurate annotations while maintaining efficient resource allocation. The proposed approach serves as a model for selecting qualified annotators in other complex annotation endeavors.

Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, has seen escalating interest, with researchers focusing on addressing its core challenges, including inadequate video signal quality, substantial domain gap, and inefficient attention distribution. Current state-of-the-art models, primarily based on pre-trained video-longformer, still encounter unresolved issues and fail to perfectly solve these problems. This paper presents a novel retrieval framework, tailored to handle text-video data with token shift, selection, and uneven attention distribution. Our proposed model employs a multi-sampled token structure with shifted and weighted token selection, paired with a cross-modal feature learning module and a unified video-longformer encoder. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on MSRVTT, HL-VIRAT, VideoCLEF, and MediaEval benchmarks, while also significantly reducing computation and memory requirements. Code and model resources are publicly available at https://github.com/ShauckJ/TS2-Net.

We've found that neutral flavour-changing currents in top sector physics, linked to electroweak scale particles that interact with leptons, can emerge naturally from a specific type of theory that involves a new type of fermion, known as fermionology. This has led us to discover new interactions involving flavour change, such as $u \rightarrow c \ell \bar{\ell}'$, that can be investigated experimentally through the study of rare top decays. We've shown how to identify unique and potentially distinctive patterns in these events and establish connections with high-energy collisions, such as those found in LHC four-top production. This has given us new opportunities to test the theories at both lower-energy and high-energy levels, using experiments with a high precision, such as those at the LHC, muon colliders, the FCC-ee, CEvI, and the future muon colliders, while also discussing potential constraints on these models from various experiments.

In response to the intricacies of network data, a new type of hybrid network is suggested that blends rules for preferential attachment and uniform attachment.  The proposed method begins with a seed graph, where it strategically adds new vertices.  Existing vertices then choose among themselves with their current degrees as the basis for connections, with a cut-off that differentiates between existing and new vertices, where the latter are connected through a uniform mechanism.  The application of this method yields hybrid networks that display a mix of the characteristics of pure preferential attachment networks and uniform networks, as revealed through the analysis of their topological properties.  A practical hybrid network was generated by the researchers to mimic the complex structure of the worldwide air transportation system, showcasing its effectiveness.  Additionally, the researchers analyzed how the hybrid networks evolve over time, finding through simulations that their characteristics change predictably over time.  A theoretical model supporting these findings was derived and an investigation into the sensitivity of the hybrid transport network to new airports showed that it closely mimics the real-world transport system.  Overall, the researchers demonstrated that their directed hybrid networks successfully capture the intricacies of real-world networks through a combination of simple rules.

The expanding utilization of unlicensed frequency bands necessitates dependable interference management systems and hence reliable identification of wireless interference (WII). Our research proposes a novel WII technique that uses a deep convolutional neural network to accurately identify multiple co-channel interference signals (from IEEE 802.15.1, IEEE 802.11 b/g and IEEE 802.15.4) amidst a signal currently in use. The technique leverages the unique characteristics of each signal to create a distinctive pattern which can then be accurately predicted. The technique achieved an impressive 99.9% multi-label identification accuracy when signaled samples were prolonged and 97.1% when signal durations were short. Furthermore, the technique's small size allows it to be executed quickly, with a processing speed of approximately 6.7 milliseconds and a memory requirement of just 676KB. The technique's effectiveness was demonstrated using a wireless sensor network application where it successfully coexisting IEEE 802.15.4 and IEEE 802.11 b/g signals without any data loss over a 85 dB signal-to-noise ratio.

To grasp the impact of gravitational forces on both quantum systems moving at varying speeds and stationary systems, we must rely on accurate quantum mechanics theories. This project involves rectifying the inaccuracies in previous quantum mechanics interpretations, eliminating extraneous calculations and parameters that had complicated the analysis. We introduce more accurate methodologies, leveraging symmetries and anti-symmetries, and utilize KG wave functions, energy operators, and other relevant tools to establish a more coherent approach. This more accurate methodology is demonstrated with a non-relativistic particle, for which we accurately calculate key observables without resorting to approximations or outdated concepts. We then apply this new methodology to analyze stationary particles, eliminating the need for inaccurate methods like the Gaussian model, and derive precise expressions for observables like displacement and energy. We conclude by rectifying a separate misconception from a previous study and successfully resolving a key problem, providing a comprehensive solution.
Countable, locally standard measure algebras are parameterized by a pair of Steinitz numbers, consisting of one value which equals or exceeds 1.

Parton distributions that account for quark and gluon correlations in a proton can be understood by analyzing specific interactions between a proton and a photon in lepton-proton collisions. Researchers in the field of lepton-proton scattering are planning to explore such correlations through the study of dedicated DVCS events, a particular type of interaction where a lepton scatters off a proton's already excited state, called the yield, as opposed to the more typical deep-inelastic scattering where the initial proton state is not involved, referred to as the cross-term. The analysis presents an innovative method to distinguish between DVCS yield and cross-term events by measuring the direction and speed of the proton's movement following the interaction, a property not easily determined in other scattering experiments. The new method's potential to study parton distributions in a more detailed way is reviewed, including its applicability to various different experimental setups such as Jefferson Lab's Experiment E12-16-001 and the proposed Electron-Ion Collider.

All industries are likely to be impacted by artificial intelligence, which has become a highly sought-after area of study in both practical and theoretical terms. Yet, researchers have yet to provide a definitive understanding of what AI entails. This paper seeks to establish a foundational model, distinguishing augmented intelligence that is enhanced through computer-based methods from other forms of intelligence. Furthermore, we explore the implications of computer-based methods of intelligence enhancement on societal and individual dynamics. To achieve this, we develop a multi-faceted framework that incorporates psychological, societal, and engineering aspects, examining respective augmentations in distinct settings and evaluating various computer-based intervention techniques. Through this framework, we highlight essential considerations that researchers and practitioners working in this field should address to ensure intelligent systems promote human well-being.

Our research involves exploring the thermal behavior of the Bose-Hubbard model in the presence of strong spin-orbit coupling originating from a mean-field state. By introducing a spin-orbit coupling term, $\mathcal{J}\sum_{i}\left(\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{i}\hat{\hat{\phi}}_x\hat{b}_i+\text{h.c.}\right)$, where $\mathcal{J}$ is a parameter that can be adjusted, into the Hamiltonian of the model, we study its impact on the phase diagram of the model. The type of spin-orbit coupling used here is distinct from that in previous studies as it does not involve random or external magnetic fields, rather it arises as a result of the mean-field interaction among bosons. As a result, new phases and behaviors emerge in the system. By analyzing the model's phase diagram, we identify three distinct regions: a region in which superfluid phases coexist with density fluctuations, a region in which density and spin superfluid phases exist independently, and a region in which spin-orbit coupling is negligible. Additionally, the theoretical results predict a wide variety of unique phase transitions that can be observed through measurements of the condensate momentum, density correlations, and Luttinger parameters. The predictions of our research can be verified through experiments performed on Bose-Hubbard model in the ultracold regime using cold bosonic atoms.

Consider two groups of finite order: G1 and G2. We define a graph with vertex set as the combined integer set, and two vertices are connected by an edge if their difference belongs to the group G1. A similar graph can be defined with the group G2. Our study involves analyzing graphs of this type and their properties, especially those that are connected or have specific spectral characteristics. We find a chain of group operations that leads to reduced graphs with diminished vertex order, while maintaining their connectivity or eigenvalue properties. Our method also enables the creation of a continuous degeneration of graphs leading to their limit object. Our main finding applies to graphs related to non-prime finite groups of order.

Recent breakthroughs in AdS/CFT correspondence research, specifically in low-dimensional settings, are explored, concentrating on AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ and AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ dualities within massive Type IIA string theory. We first examine the solutions derived in 1908.09851 of AdS$_3$ supergravity, coupled with supersymmetry $\mathcal{N}=(0,4)$. These 2d CFT duals are re-evaluated as being equivalent to the theory of super-Wedge inclusions within the context of four super-Neveu-Salmberger strings. Next, the solutions derived in 2009.09934 as AdS$_2$ supergravity, paired with supersymmetry $\mathcal{N}=4$, are discussed in further detail. These solutions have the potential to advance our understanding regarding the holographic dual of a quantum field theory, specifically one with supersymmetry $\mathcal{N}=4$, through the re-examination of its classical action. Additionally, the action's super-oscillatory properties are explicitly calculated and the underlying reasons for its observed symmetry are presented. We conclude with a re-presentation of the solutions' salient characteristics in a simplified, tabulated format.

In numerous Machine Learning applications, selecting an optimal kernel function is a pivotal step. Gaussian Processes excel in regression and classification tasks, largely depending on a well-suited kernel function. Traditionally, Gaussian Process researchers have either designed kernels from scratch, picked them from a predetermined list, or systematically searched for kernel compositions within pre-defined parameter spaces. This paper innovatively leverages Genetic-Programming, utilizing trees of fundamental mathematical expressions to represent kernel functions, thereby broadening the potential solutions, though also introducing new complexities. Our proposed method can successfully address these challenges and uncover kernel models accurately reflecting data properties. Empirically validated on real-world time-series extrapolation problems, this method surpassed state-of-the-art performance while decreasing kernel intricacy.

Future high-energy muon colliders face a challenge due to in-flight decays of
muons from the beam line, resulting in beam-induced backgrounds (BIB). The
collider's detector design must be able to handle BIB to 1-100 picoseconds,
depending on the energy reach and detector technology. To mitigate BIB, the
detector can utilize BAGAN, an end-cap detector design that shields the
detector with a 2 mm plastic scintillator, achieving a BIB reduction of two
orders of magnitude. Metal detectors can also provide BIB reduction by
encapsulating the beam inside the detector, however this design may not be
suitable for high-energy reaches due to size constraints. Metal detectors with
in-flight muon stopping capabilities can also provide BIB reduction. The end-cap
design with in-flight muon stopping metal detector technology may offer the best
solution, enabling BIB reduction of two orders of magnitude while allowing the
detector to fully capture muons for analysis, thus providing the highest
detectable luminosity and overall efficiency.

Introducing Spartan, a novel approach for training neural networks with pre-defined sparsity. This method effectively leverages a combination of two techniques: soft parameter pruning through optimal transportation and hard parameter sparsification during forward passes. This dynamic balance enables initial exploration of various sparsity patterns and eventually converges to the desired pattern. Spartan offers flexibility in incorporating diverse sparsity policies, is simple to implement, and runs efficiently. thoroughsparsity, a related method for evaluating network sparsity, is also presented. Spartan demonstrates exceptional performance on both MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, achieving sparsity in both weight and activation layers. This research is now publicly accessible on arXiv.

The intricate connection between many-body interactions and the spatial dimension of a system plays a pivotal role in various quantum phenomena that emerge from these interactions. A compelling example of this relationship is the behavior of a Bose gas confined to a one-dimensional space, where the presence of an infinite number of conservation laws prevents the system from reaching thermal equilibrium and constraining the system's dynamics. In this study, we examine the dynamics following the initialization of a one-dimensional Bose gas that has been prepared in a highly excited state with a non-zero life expectancy. By incorporating an analytical approach, we identify a novel phenomenon where many-body interactions give rise to a temporal barrier for the system's evolution, preventing it from accessing higher energy states, even when the system is weakly interacting. Notably, we demonstrate that the duration of this barrier, and the maximum number of higher energy states that can be accessed, increase proportionally with the size of the system. Furthermore, using exact numerical calculations for up to 37 particles in a closed chain, we provide complementary evidence for this phenomenon, and its connection to the influence of entanglement and the importance of the relative phase between various energy levels, that is, the Franck-Condon factor. By exploring the decay patterns of the system at different energy levels, we shed light on the role of entanglement and the system's many-body interactions, and propose a general explanation for this phenomenon that extends beyond the system's specific parameters, providing a unified perspective that incorporates both mean-field theory

Software developers widely acknowledge the importance of unit testing as a critical aspect of their work cycle, allowing for swift detection and resolution of coding errors. However, decades of empirical research have revealed that various common issues can compromise the effectiveness and integrity of test code, necessitating special attention. These problematic patterns are termed 'test smells,' identified through specific criteria that help developers pinpoint and eliminate them to produce high-quality test code. Studies on test smells have typically been conducted by researchers, with little insight gained from the perspective of professional developers. To gain a deeper understanding of developers' perspectives, a quantitative study was undertaken to ask developers about the severity of specific test smells in Java code; the survey gathered extensive data, with 152 participants sharing their views. The analysis of the collected responses revealed some surprising findings that challenge the conventional wisdom of researchers on the priority order of test smells, highlighting potential differences between the perspectives of researchers and practicing developers.

This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a modified version of the sweeping process, first proposed by J.J. Moreau in the early 1970s as part of plasticity theory. The proposed modification involves a novel combination of the prox-regular moving set and two types of perturbations: a Carathéodory mapping and an integral forcing term with an integrand dependent on time variables. To address this challenge, a new, residual continuous step is introduced, along with a compactness argument in the a priori estimation, to prove the main results. Additionally, the paper introduces two concrete examples of sets, namely, convex polyhedral and spherical moving sets, to demonstrate their applicability to the sweeping process, with the former corresponding to Sigalov's problem and the latter to a classical problem in the history of variational history-dependent problem theory.

We introduce the updated version of the {\tt KKMCee} event generator, version 5.00.2, designed for simulating lepton and quark pair production through high-energy electron-positron annihilations. As the most advanced generator for this process, the code, now rewritten entirely in modern C++, maintains all features of its Fortran 77 predecessor, while incorporating several enhanced Monte Carlo algorithmic improvements. Its capabilities, supplemented with the ability to create polarized final-state particles, allow for the generation of comprehensive event lists according to various creation mechanisms, including the Standard Model, heavy lepton models, contact interactions and other non-standard models. The {\tt KKMCee} event generator, accessible through the {\tt CMSSW} framework, connects to {\tt PHOTOS} for realistic photon emissions, can utilize {\tt BRAHMS} for precise heavy-particle decays and is integrated with {\tt CLHEP}, ensuring for accurate real-number calculations. The paper outlines the underlying software architecture, highlights its key functionalities and illustrates its performance through a detailed example. The {\tt KKMCee} event generator, downloadable from CERN's software repository, enables researchers to create high-quality simulations for a range of physics models and advance their understanding of particle physics at advanced lepton colliders.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular issues. However, the signal quality may deteriorate due to various factors like noise and alterations, hindering the accurate estimation of inter-beat intervals. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel approach utilizing the Tiramisu model for accurate estimation of inter-beat intervals, even in noisy and degraded signal conditions. By leveraging the capabilities of semi-supervised learning and incorporating a custom-made target loss function, our proposed method outperforms existing estimators with a higher peak signal-to-noise ratio by at least 4 decibels and a lower error rate of 9%.

To utilize contemporary computing systems efficiently, an important consideration is the minimal number of data accesses necessary for processing operations. A randomized algorithm, which determines matrix singular values with significantly fewer accesses, has been developed using a small number of passes per data element. This method has been enhanced by employing a higher-order singular value decomposition technique, which calculates all singular values of a tensor with three dimensions using approximately 2n passes, but due to memory constraints, this approach becomes impractical for large tensor dimensions. In contrast, a recently introduced approach allows computing the largest singular values of a tensor with 3n/2 or more passes, but a significant challenge remains determining all singular values. Another significant issue arises from memory limitations preventing the use of an all-to-all data communication approach within tensor computation. A solution to this problem has been developed by employing an out-of-core memory strategy that enables a more efficient memory usage of O(n^2) with associated all-to-all data accesses of O(n^3), but this remains a highly optimized memory solution. Nevertheless, a solution to the original problem has been obtained by employing a more efficient random sampling approach along with a more efficient data redistribution algorithm, which achieve better results than the previously used methods. Specifically, these new algorithms require O(n^2) memory accesses and an all-to-all data transfer of O(n^3), but with fewer data accesses and a more efficient data transfer than previous random sampling approaches.
